title: sklearn.callbacks._transport.open_listener should document thread-safety requirements
body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The `message_consumer` callable argument to `sklearn.callbacks._transport.open_listener()` can be called from multiple threads within the same process, when using a thread pool instead of a process pool. That means it needs to be thread-safe.

In practice all callers are actually thread-safe, so that's not a problem.

However, this requirement is not documented.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a note saying that the `message_consumer` might be called from multiple different threads and must be prepared to handle this correctly.

I'm happy to do this.
author: itamarst

comments.author: jeremiedbb
comments.body: That's correct, the message_consumer is expected to be thread safe. A improvement of the docstring of `open_listener` is welcome.

comments.author: Git169-hub
comments.body:
Hi, I looked into this issue and cloned the current main branch to check. The thread-safety requirement for message_consumer is already documented in the current docstring for open_listener in sklearn/callback/_transport.py:
"This callable may be called from multiple different threads, and must therefore behave in a thread-safe manner."
It looks like this was already addressed. Could a maintainer confirm if this issue can be closed?

title: BUG: LinearRegression is wrong on float32 and large n_samples (> 500k rows) due to `cond` param to scipy.linalg.lstsq
body:
### Describe the bug

`LinearRegression` is wrong on `float32` with a large sample size (e.g. 500k rows) since sklearn 1.6.0. This is still the case on 1.8.0. See minimal repro below. The residual sum of squares is much larger than the solution found by `{scipy,numpy}.linalg.lstsq` on `float32`.

Using the minimal repro below, `git bisect` points to this commit from https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/30040: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/bef9d1803d1f243e4d3f9e845fac356a4fc555a8

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/66200f149ba6c64a3a93dd73e37bdeea87bb5db8/sklearn/linear_model/_base.py#L702-L703

- Indeed, changing L702 to `cond = None` fixes the bug.
    - Doing so will revive issue #26164, so someone needs to make a call.
    - I think issue 26164 is strictly less important than the correctness of linear regression (minimize residue).
- `cond` at L702 scales up linearly with the number of rows and eventually zeros out large enough singular values to throw off the solution completely.
- As a result, sklearn `LinearRegression` fails to scale to even 500k rows at `float32` precision below.
- Meanwhile, `scipy.linalg.lstsq` (the underlying solver) and `numpy.linalg.lstsq` don't have this issue with the internally defaulted `cond` / `rcond` values (see inline comments below).

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python3
import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

np.random.seed(1337)
n_samples = 500_000

x1 = np.random.rand(n_samples)
x2 = 0.3 * x1 + 0.1 * np.random.rand(n_samples)
X = np.column_stack([x1, x2])
y = X @ [0.5, 2.0] + 0.1 * np.random.rand(n_samples)
assert X.dtype == np.float64 and y.dtype == np.float64

X32, y32 = X.astype(np.float32), y.astype(np.float32)

scipy_f64 = linalg.lstsq(X, y)[0]
scipy_f32 = linalg.lstsq(X32, y32)[0]  # pdb -> cond defaults to np.float32(1.1920929e-07)
numpy_f64 = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y)[0]
numpy_f32 = np.linalg.lstsq(X32, y32)[0]  # pdb -> rcond defaults to np.float64(1.1102230246251565e-10)
sklearn_f64 = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(X, y).coef_
sklearn_f32 = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(X32, y32).coef_  # pdb -> sklearn sets cond to np.float32(0.059604645)

print(f"scipy float64:    {scipy_f64}, residue: {linalg.norm(y - X @ scipy_f64):.2f}")
print(f"scipy float32:    {scipy_f32}, residue: {linalg.norm(y32 - X32 @ scipy_f32):.2f}")
print(f"numpy float64:    {numpy_f64}, residue: {linalg.norm(y - X @ numpy_f64):.2f}")
print(f"numpy float32:    {numpy_f32}, residue: {linalg.norm(y32 - X32 @ numpy_f32):.2f}")
print(f"sklearn float64:  {sklearn_f64}, residue: {linalg.norm(y - X @ sklearn_f64):.2f}")
print(f"sklearn float32:  {sklearn_f32}, residue: {linalg.norm(y32 - X32 @ sklearn_f32):.2f}  <--------")
```

### Expected Results

```python3
scipy float64:    [0.41391995 2.42901607], residue: 24.40
scipy float32:    [0.4139197 2.429016 ], residue: 24.40
numpy float64:    [0.41391995 2.42901607], residue: 24.40
numpy float32:    [0.41391996 2.429016  ], residue: 24.40
sklearn float64:  [0.41391995 2.42901607], residue: 24.40
sklearn float32:  [0.4139197 2.429016 ], residue: 24.40  <--------
```

### Actual Results

```python3
scipy float64:    [0.41391995 2.42901607], residue: 24.40
scipy float32:    [0.4139197 2.429016 ], residue: 24.40
numpy float64:    [0.41391995 2.42901607], residue: 24.40
numpy float32:    [0.41391996 2.429016  ], residue: 24.40
sklearn float64:  [0.41391995 2.42901607], residue: 24.40
sklearn float32:  [1.1635013  0.43804753], residue: 59.06  <--------
```


### Root cause analysis

Why does sklearn set `cond` this way in the first place? [#30040](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/30040) explains:
> The `scipy.linalg.lstsq` solver can fail the sample weight consistency test, especially for wide dataset (`n_features > n_samples`) after centering `X,y` (as done when `fit_intercept=True`).
> 
> Setting the `cond` parameter (cut-off ratio on singular values) to the value recommended by `numpy.linalg.lstsq` documentation seems to fix the bug.
- Indeed, `numpy.linalg.lstsq` defaults to [`rcond = finfo(t).eps * max(n, m)`](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.4.0/numpy/linalg/_linalg.py#L2528-L2529)
    - However, for float32 input, numpy sets `t` (calculation precision) to float64 and `result_t` (result precision) to float32 ([two  lines above](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.4.0/numpy/linalg/_linalg.py#L2525)), so numpy does not have the bug described by the current issue.
        - Calc type is always float64: [here](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.4.1/numpy/linalg/_linalg.py#L206-L210) and [there (`signature = 'ddd->ddid'`)](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.4.1/numpy/linalg/_linalg.py#L2525-L2531).
        - This comes at a cost. float32 X will be cast into a float64 copy by numpy's [ufunc `signature` mechanism](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/ufuncs.html):
            - > Casting will be used as necessary. The actual DType of the input arrays is not considered unless signature is None for that array.
    - sklearn's underlying solver is `scipy.linalg.lstsq`. For float32 input, it sets calculation precision to `float32` (no casting / copy), unlike numpy's `float64`.
        - This does not interact well with `numpy's` default `rcond`, resulting in this bug.
    - The above can be validated by pdb-ing into the corresponding lines in the minimal repro above.

### Suggested fix

First add the above minimal repro as a new test case.

Then add `float32` to #30040's test case `test_linear_regression_sample_weight_consistency` with this patch:
<details>

<summary>Click to expand patch!</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py b/sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py
index a1b7c79e6f..9d4982f52e 100644
--- a/sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py
+++ b/sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py
@@ -762,8 +762,9 @@ def test_fused_types_make_dataset(csr_container):
     ],
 )
 @pytest.mark.parametrize("fit_intercept", [False, True])
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("dtype", [np.float32, np.float64])
 def test_linear_regression_sample_weight_consistency(
-    X_shape, sparse_container, fit_intercept, global_random_seed
+    X_shape, sparse_container, fit_intercept, dtype, global_random_seed
 ):
     """Test that the impact of sample_weight is consistent.
 
@@ -774,8 +775,8 @@ def test_linear_regression_sample_weight_consistency(
     rng = np.random.RandomState(global_random_seed)
     n_samples, n_features = X_shape
 
-    X = rng.rand(n_samples, n_features)
-    y = rng.rand(n_samples)
+    X = rng.rand(n_samples, n_features).astype(dtype)
+    y = rng.rand(n_samples).astype(dtype)
     if sparse_container is not None:
         X = sparse_container(X)
     params = dict(fit_intercept=fit_intercept)
@@ -790,14 +791,14 @@ def test_linear_regression_sample_weight_consistency(
     # test with sparse input.
     sample_weight = np.ones_like(y)
     reg.fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight)
-    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef, rtol=1e-6)
+    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef, rtol=1e-3 if dtype == np.float32 else 1e-6)
     if fit_intercept:
         assert_allclose(reg.intercept_, intercept)
 
     # 2) sample_weight=None should be equivalent to sample_weight = number
     sample_weight = 123.0
     reg.fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight)
-    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef, rtol=1e-6)
+    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef, rtol=1e-3 if dtype == np.float32 else 1e-6)
     if fit_intercept:
         assert_allclose(reg.intercept_, intercept)
 
@@ -809,7 +810,8 @@ def test_linear_regression_sample_weight_consistency(
         intercept = reg.intercept_
 
     reg.fit(X, y, sample_weight=np.pi * sample_weight)
-    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef, rtol=1e-6 if sparse_container is None else 1e-5)
+    rtol = 1e-3 if dtype == np.float32 else 1e-6 if sparse_container is None else 1e-5
+    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef, rtol=rtol)
     if fit_intercept:
         assert_allclose(reg.intercept_, intercept)
 
@@ -822,7 +824,7 @@ def test_linear_regression_sample_weight_consistency(
     if fit_intercept:
         intercept_0 = reg.intercept_
     reg.fit(X[:-5], y[:-5], sample_weight=sample_weight[:-5])
-    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef_0, rtol=1e-5)
+    assert_allclose(reg.coef_, coef_0, rtol=3e-3 if dtype == np.float32 else 1e-5)
     if fit_intercept:
         assert_allclose(reg.intercept_, intercept_0)
 
@@ -841,7 +843,7 @@ def test_linear_regression_sample_weight_consistency(
 
     reg1 = LinearRegression(**params).fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight_1)
     reg2 = LinearRegression(**params).fit(X2, y2, sample_weight=sample_weight_2)
-    assert_allclose(reg1.coef_, reg2.coef_, rtol=1e-6)
+    assert_allclose(reg1.coef_, reg2.coef_, rtol=1e-3 if dtype == np.float32 else 1e-6)
     if fit_intercept:
         assert_allclose(reg1.intercept_, reg2.intercept_)
 
```

</details>

Then do TDD to find a combination of (dtype, cond) to pass all tests. I haven't been able to find anything reasonable.

I think it is more urgent to fix `LinearRegression` to meet its definition (minimize residue sum of squares) than to pass the [sample weight consistency tests](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/762734097daa72f6bd1b363ac989afa4717530f7/sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py#L765). In the worst case I recommend setting `cond = None`, marking the weight tests as xfail, reopening #26164, and maybe report #26164 upstream (to scipy).

title: Add a contributor introduction to the PR template
body:
I noticed that numpy recently updated their PR template (https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/30932) which now includes a section where the contributor should introduce himself (if first time contributor). I found that quite interesting for our struggle with the flood of fully automated PRs.

They added the following instruction
``` 
### First time committer introduction
<!-- If you are new to the NumPy community, please introduce yourself. How do you
 use NumPy, what prompted you to make this contribution? We are a community of
 mostly volunteers, and getting to know you helps us trust your judgement
 and welcome you into the community. 
-->
```

What do you think ?
author: jeremiedbb

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body: I like that a lot. It can make the interaction more personal and fruitful (in the best case) and help us judge how much time we can invest in mentoring a new person.

title: MDS can return wrong number of components when using ClassicalMDS initialization
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using the new `init="classical_mds"` option in `MDS`, the number of components returned is always 2.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.manifold import MDS

data = np.random.uniform(size=(20, 10))

model = MDS(init="classical_mds", n_components=3, n_init=1)

transformed_data = model.fit_transform(data)

print("Output n_components:", transformed_data.shape[1])
```

Output n_components: 3

title: Consider switching to pyrefly for typechecking
body:
I'd like to propose adding [Pyrefly](https://pyrefly.org) for typechecking - it could either be added alongside mypy as a non-blocking CI check or migrated entirely. Happy to open the PR, checking here first to see if there's interest?

For transparency I work on the Pyrefly team, I've been looking into the performance of mypy vs Pyrefly on real repos and when I tried out sklearn the results looked promising enough that I thought I'd share :)

I did some initial investigation, running locally mypy 2.3.0 vs Pyrefly 1.1.1 (checking `sklearn/`) which shows Pyrefly is ~29x faster:

  | Checker   | Run        |
  |-----------|------------|
  | mypy      | **18.4 s** |
  | Pyrefly   | **0.6 s**  |


## How to make the switch:

  1. **Add the dependency** to the test/lint requirements: `pyrefly>=1.1.1`.
  2. **Add `[tool.pyrefly]` config** mirroring the existing `[tool.mypy]` config.
     ```toml
     [tool.pyrefly]
     project-includes = ["sklearn"]                        # matches `mypy sklearn/` in build_tools/linting.sh
     search-path = ["."]
     project-excludes = ["**/sklearn/externals*"]          # mirrors mypy's exclude
     preset = "legacy"                                      # matches mypy's non-strict defaults
     ignore-missing-imports = ["joblib.*", "sklearn.externals.*", "*"]  # mirrors ignore_missing_imports + follow_imports=skip
     ```
  3. **resolve/suppress error code differences** There are some differences between the errors pyrefly catches and what mypy does (79 new errors from what I can see running locally, details below), so we could either ignore them  (`# pyrefly: ignore [code]`) for now or see if there are genuine issues to address. If we opt for removing mypy we could also remove ~80 out of 82 mypy ignores that pyrefly doesn't complain about, so the total ignores would stay roughly the same.
  4. **Setup in CI** in .github/workflows/lint.yml (`build_tools/linting.sh`), mirroring the mypy
     step with a run pyrefly check step.

## Error differences - Mypy vs Pyrefly

  When I compared pyrefly and mypy output, I found 79 new errors from Pyrefly that aren't flagged by Mypy. Some might be real typing issues that should be resolved, but I'm not super familiar with the sklearn codebase so would require some deeper investigation. Here's a summary of the differences:

  | Error code | Count | Reason for difference | Suggested approach |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `bad-override` | 72 | Estimator subclasses override base `fit`/`transform`/callback methods with looser signatures than Pyrefly's LSP-override check allows — 54 in `sklearn/` (mostly `cluster/*`), 18 in tests. Pyright/mypy are more permissive here. | Suppress - looks mostly benign; could align a few signatures over time |
  | `missing-attribute` | 3 | `pytest` narrowed to `None` via the optional-import guard in `estimator_checks.py` (`.mark`/`.param`) | Suppress |
  | `bad-argument-type` | 1 | `_openml.py:716` | **Review** and consider fixing |
  | `no-matching-overload` | 1 | `_metadata_requests.py:1668` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | `unsupported-operation` | 1 | `instance_generator.py:1356` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | `missing-argument` | 1 | `estimator_checks.py:956` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | **Total** | **79** | | **~75 suppress · ~4 review** |
author: javabster

comments.author: hiSandog
comments.body: A non-blocking trial is safer than an immediate migration. Please compare wall time/incremental behavior, diagnostics and false positives on the existing codebase, supported typing features/plugins, configuration differences, and editor integration; record both tools' pinned versions. A small acceptance criterion—same or better actionable coverage with an agreed performance gain—would keep the evaluation objective.

We actually considered it in [this PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32737), but closed it again due to a lack of responses from other maintainers. title: Support infinite values in DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees (now that NaN is supported)
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Hello,

I am facing a problem where the proper handling of infinite values would be helpful. Since the introduction of the support for missing values (#23595/#26391/#27966), I was wondering to what extent it would be possible to handle those.

Currently:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [np.inf], [10.0]])
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]
DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X, y)
# ValueError: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float32').
```

This is because infinite value is explicitly rejected regardless, in `BaseDecisionTree._compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask` (`sklearn/tree/_classes.py`):
A second guard in `_validate_X_predict` (same file) does the same at predict time.

```
if not np.isfinite(overall_sum):
    # Raise a ValueError in case of the presence of an infinite element.
    _assert_all_finite_element_wise(X, xp=np, allow_nan=True, **common_kwargs)
```

Both guards live on `BaseDecisionTree`, shared by all four tree classes; `RandomForest*`/`ExtraTrees*` call the same method rather than duplicating it. 

`GradientBoostingClassifier`/`Regressor` don't set `allow_nan` and aren't affected either way. Small number of call sites.

### Describe your proposed solution

The splitter already tolerates infinite values without modification. Unlike NaN, +inf/-inf are ordinary totally-ordered floats (-inf < finite < +inf), so <= comparisons already place them correctly, with no new split-evaluation logic needed like NaN required. Verified by monkeypatching out just the two guards: DecisionTreeClassifier fits and predicts correctly on +inf/-inf data, including placing a real split threshold at -inf. Checked sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx too: thresholds are computed as feature_values[p_prev]/2.0 + feature_values[p]/2.0 (sum-of-halves, to avoid overflow on large finite values), with a fallback to feature_values[p_prev] if the result lands exactly on +INFINITY/-INFINITY. With real -inf in the data this fallback is a no-op (-inf sorts first, so the fallback value is -inf too).

check_estimators_nan_inf (the common test for this) is already skipped entirely for these estimators (gated by one allow_nan tag covering both NaN and inf), so relaxing the guard doesn't remove existing coverage, though new tests would need to be added for inf specifically. Proposal: relax the two guards (behind allow_nan or a new dedicated tag), and add that dedicated inf/NaN test coverage.

title: CI : Numerical flakiness in test_enet_ols_consistency
body:
### Describe the bug

While working on another scikit-learn PR (**#32368**), CI intermittently failed in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_coordinate_descent.py::test_enet_ols_consistency`.It came from a strict numerical ordering assertion on the squared error:

```python
assert se_enet <= se_ols <= 1e-20
```

This was recently merged 2 days ago in #32845 . On further digging, I noticed:

* the squared error is computed **without `sample_weight`**, even though both models are fit with `sample_weight`
* Lot of tests in this test file are using a **hard-coded RNG seed** (`RandomState(42)`) instead of `global_random_seed` ( I did have a look at #22827 ) 
* when running across multiple seeds (e.g. with `SKLEARN_TESTS_GLOBAL_RANDOM_SEED=all`), additional failures can appear for some configurations due to **tight absolute tolerances** on `intercept_` comparisons near zero.

P.S Same test was passing for seed 42 on Windows locally. However as i start changing seeds it would fail on Windows too. 


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

I updated this test to use `global_random_seed` and ran it for all seeds on Ubuntu. 

```bash
SKLEARN_TESTS_GLOBAL_RANDOM_SEED=all pytest sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_coordinate_descent.py -k test_enet_ols_consistency
```


```python
@pytest.mark.filterwarnings("ignore:With alpha=0, this algorithm:UserWarning")
@pytest.mark.parametrize("precompute", [False, True])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("effective_rank", [None, 10])
def test_enet_ols_consistency(precompute, effective_rank,global_random_seed):
    """Test that ElasticNet(alpha=0) converges to the same solution as OLS."""
    rng = np.random.RandomState(global_random_seed)
    n_samples = 300
    X, y = make_regression(
        n_samples=n_samples,
        n_features=100,
        effective_rank=effective_rank,
        n_informative=50,
        random_state=rng,
    )
    sw = rng.uniform(low=0.01, high=10, size=X.shape[0])

    ols = LinearRegression().fit(X, y, sample_weight=sw)
    enet = ElasticNet(alpha=0, precompute=precompute, tol=1e-15).fit(
        X, y, sample_weight=sw
    )

    # Might be a singular problem, so check for same predictions
    assert_allclose(enet.predict(X), ols.predict(X))
    # and for similar objective function (squared error)
    se_ols = np.sum((y - ols.predict(X)) ** 2)
    se_enet = np.sum((y - enet.predict(X)) ** 2)
    if precompute:
        assert se_ols <= 1e-20
        assert se_enet <= 1e-20
    else:
        assert se_enet <= se_ols <= 1e-20  # Who would have thought that?
    # We check equal coefficients, but "only" with absolute tolerance.
    assert_allclose(enet.coef_, ols.coef_, atol=1e-11)
    assert_allclose(enet.intercept_, ols.intercept_, atol=1e-12)
```

No test failures

title: BUG undefined `n_classes` for custom estimators in `DecisionBoundaryDisplay`
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When introducing `n_classes` for the `DecisionBoundaryDisplay` in  https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33015, we didn't think about custom estimators like in [this example](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/auto_examples/cluster/plot_inductive_clustering.html) (re-created in the minimal example below), where `n_classes` can not be extracted from the estimator without knowing its architecture, which currently breaks [CircleCI](https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/scikit-learn/scikit-learn?branch=main).
(@lesteve, just so you know we're fixing it!)

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, clone
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import DecisionBoundaryDisplay
from sklearn.utils.validation import check_is_fitted

N_SAMPLES = 5000
RANDOM_STATE = 42

class InductiveClusterer(BaseEstimator):
    def __init__(self, clusterer, classifier):
        self.clusterer = clusterer
        self.classifier = classifier

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        self.clusterer_ = clone(self.clusterer)
        self.classifier_ = clone(self.classifier)
        y = self.clusterer_.fit_predict(X)
        self.classifier_.fit(X, y)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        check_is_fitted(self)
        return self.classifier_.predict(X)

# Generate some training data from clustering
X, y = make_blobs(
    n_samples=N_SAMPLES,
    cluster_std=[1.0, 1.0, 0.5],
    centers=[(-5, -5), (0, 0), (5, 5)],
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
)

# Train a clustering algorithm on the training data and get the cluster labels
clusterer = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3)
classifier = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
inductive_learner = InductiveClusterer(clusterer, classifier).fit(X)

# Plotting decision regions
DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator(
    inductive_learner, X, response_method="predict", alpha=0.4
)
plt.show()
```

### Expected Results

Plot is shown.

### Actual Results

`UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'n_classes' where it is not associated with a value`

### Versions

```shell
sklearn: 1.9.dev0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

I don't think there is a sensible default value we could assume in these cases. My suggestion would be to add `n_classes=None` as a default parameter to `from_estimator` and raise a `ValueError` if it cannot be inferred from the estimator and has not been specified.
If you agree @ogrisel, @lucyleeow, I'll open a PR for this.
author: AnneBeyer

comments.author: lucyleeow
comments.body:
I'm not sure what the best option is. Looking at the `is_regressor` / `is_clusterer` etc functions - they are just checking for the presence of the relevant estimator tag.

Looking at our docs for [developing your own estimator](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#rolling-your-own-estimator) we do have a section suggesting use of estimator [tags](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#estimator-tags) (though of course this can't be relied on). There is also a section recommending use of our mixins (and ducktyping for checking type of estimator):

> We tend to use “duck typing” instead of checking for [isinstance](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#isinstance), which means it’s technically possible to implement an estimator without inheriting from scikit-learn classes. However, if you don’t inherit from the right mixins, either there will be a large amount of boilerplate code for you to implement and keep in sync with scikit-learn development, or your estimator might not function the same way as a scikit-learn estimator.

I think we could do some more inferring before we error - here are some suggestions (not mutually exclusive):

* add the appropriate estimator tag to the estimator, in the example - this only fixes the example of course, but it is probably nice to demonstrate use of tags (which is what we recommend) in our own examples
* we could add ducktyping i.e. `is_regressor or isinstance(estimator, RegressorMixin)` - this will pick up more cases, but again not all
* add an `else` condition (to the logic where we infer `n_classes` in `from_estimator`) where we do `type_of_target` on `y` and infer type and then use `unique` to get `n_classes` if relevant - `type_of_target` is not always accurate but it gives reasonable results

@lesteve and @ogrisel may have more suggestions / thoughts to add though.

comments.body:
Since it is breaking CI, I would be in favour of a quick solution first.
I'll open a PR with a suggestion for adding an error and the missing test and a fix for the example.
I'm happy to iterate on the possible inferring options afterwards.

title: DOC: Modernize and improve examples in train_test_split
body:
### Current Problem

The examples in `train_test_split` (`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py`) mix old NumPy-style output with pandas DataFrames, but the pandas part is not very clear or modern.

Many new users expect to see how the function behaves with DataFrames (column names and index are preserved, etc.).

### Why it matters
`train_test_split` is one of the most commonly used functions in scikit-learn. Clear, modern examples help users understand the expected behavior, especially when working with pandas DataFrames.

### Proposed Improvement

- Update the pandas example to clearly show that column names and index are preserved in the output.
- Add one short example demonstrating the `stratify` parameter.
- Make the output more readable and consistent.

**Location**:  
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` → `train_test_split` function (Examples section)

I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this documentation improvement once the issue is triaged and approved.
author: anikchand461

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
Thanks for the issues you opened. There are already many, many high quality issues and PRs that are in need of maintainer time and attention. We expect people to put forward their best work and want to give them our best work/attention. Typically someone who is not a regular contributor and opens several issues in a short time gets seen as someone who asked their favourite AI Agent to do the work. This means maintainers will assign a "low quality" label (in their head) to your issues.

My recommendation to you is to close all but the top two issues you created and focus on making them your best work.

Once those issues have been dealt with, you can go ahead and create two more issues based on what you learnt.

This step by step approach allows you to focus on creating the best possible work you can and prevents the knee jerk reaction from maintainers to label things as "low effort, probably AI generated without human review".

comments.author: GaelVaroquaux
comments.body:
I made a simpler reproducer, only with scikit-learn transformers:
```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from skrub import DropCols
from skrub.datasets import fetch_employee_salaries

datasets = fetch_employee_salaries()

X, y = datasets.X, datasets.y

date_encoder = make_pipeline(
    DropCols("date_first_hired"),

```

As DropCols tries to be a legit scikit-learn transformer, I do think that we have an issue that we should address in scikit-learn

comments.author: GaelVaroquaux
comments.body:
OK, digging a bit more into this, I think that the problem arises because skrub.DropCols doesn't implement the scikit-learn conventions really well and thus the function sklearn.utils.validation._is_fitted doesn't detected that it is fitted.

More precisely, DropCols has the tag "requires_fit", but none of its fitted attributes end with `_`. The fact that none of its fitted attributes end with `_` is a violation of conventions, and a "bad" thing. However, I worry that it is very hard for related projects to get all our conventions right. So I think that this is something that we should address

Atomic reproducer:

```python
from sklearn.utils.validation import _is_fitted
from skrub import DropCols

from skrub.datasets import fetch_employee_salaries
datasets = fetch_employee_salaries()

X, y = datasets.X, datasets.y
model = DropCols("date_first_hired")
model.fit(X[["date_first_hired", "gender"]])

print(_is_fitted(model))
```

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
I think the immediate fix is something to do in skrub.

Coming back to the bigger question about how difficult it is to make a scikit-learn compatible estimator, so basically preventing this problem from happening in the first place.

Does `DropCols` pass the common estimator checks? Does skrub use them to "certify" the estimators that want to be scikit-learn estimators?

I agree that creating a conforming scikti-learn estimator is quite difficult - in the sense that you have to do a lot of things that are not obvious from the start and only later realise that you missed it. For example the case in this issue: it makes sense that the generic "is this fitted?" checker relies on there being a fitted attribute. But, as estimator implementor, it is not clear that you have to have a fitted attribute. Long story short, I think the common tests are the only hope in gaining confidence as estimator implementor that you got it right. This means there are two questions: are these common checks easy enough to discover and use? Do the current checks catch this problem?

If the answer is no, to either of these, there is work to be done in scikit-learn.

I don't know :). Skrub should implement this, but it not that easy (aka people need to know and understand these things).

IMHO, no. But then, it's a recurrent problem of everything in life :) : the information is often hard to find, even when it's in the middle of my desk (or worse, mailbox). I believe that we need to cater for people not finding it.


**Broader point of view** : I think that if skrub has this problem, we probably have a bunch of libraries that have it. I do think that it is worth reflecting on how to avoid that we keep breaking compatibility with a broader ecosystem

comments.author: rcap107
comments.body:
A comment unrelated from the original issue, but related to understanding the documentation. 

As I am working on skrub's transformers I keep on learning new requirements for transformers that are either not clear from the developer documentation, or are just missing. 

For example, if I have a parameter in the init that is not a dataframe or array, I am still not meant to modify it in the fit, but this is not really explicitly explained anywhere. 

I think it would be convenient to have a checklist that states all the things that an estimator should or should not do. 

Common tests are not mentioned clearly enough: in the dev guide they are called "common checks" without any reference and in a throwaway line at the end of a very long section, and in the glossary there is a fairly uninformative entry for "common tests". 

So far my experience has been going off of half comments from various maintainers, hunting for single words in the documentation, or pulling teeth out of LLMs to tell me where to look for a specific convention. 

I can tell you it is quite frustrating, and I have a far better access to maintainers to ask for clarification than most people who try to develop their own transformers.

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
You gave the answer that I was hoping for, but also dreading. From what you say about making a scikit-learn compatible estimator and what I've seen in cuml -> it is too hard to achieve this goal. I didn't comment before Christmas because I thought I should think about how we could solve this before replying. Now it is already the next year and I still have no great idea for a concrete thing to do that improves things. But so much time has passed that I should comment anyway.

Improving the documentation is clearly something to do. The hard part IMHO is how to do it so that it becomes easier to find the important information. For example, I think we should aim to make the relevant bits of documentation _shorter_, not longer as part of this work. Why shorter? Because it means it is easier to find stuff and because trying to make it shorter will counter our natural urge to "just add more information". But the details of how to do this are still unclear to me.

If we do revamp the docs and guides we should also make a blog post on the scikit-learn blog about the fact that this work has happened. Ideally repeating some of the information, because repetition is the way to get people to remember things.

If you have thoughts or want to try something out (and have the time) I think it would be good to make a PR with a proposal. Maybe too much thinking up front isn't actually all that useful?!

title: docs: document speciesist bias as recognized category in fairness documentation
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

## Proposal

Add speciesist bias as a recognized bias category in scikit-learn's fairness and bias documentation.

## Precedent Within scikit-learn

scikit-learn already took a significant step by removing the Boston Housing dataset due to racial bias (PR #20729). This demonstrated the project's commitment to addressing documented biases in ML tools and datasets.

## Academic Foundation

Speciesist bias in AI/ML is now documented across multiple peer-reviewed publications:

- **Hagendorff et al. (2023).** "Speciesist bias in AI." *AI and Ethics*. Found speciesist bias in image recognition, word embeddings, and language models.
- **Takeshita et al. (2022).** Found BERT, RoBERTa associate harmful words with nonhuman animals. *Information Processing & Management*.
- **Hagendorff et al. (2025).** SpeciesismBench (1,003 items): LLMs "frequently normalized harm toward farmed animals."

## Relevance to scikit-learn

- **Text classification**: Models trained with TF-IDF or other text features inherit speciesist associations from training corpora
- **Sentiment analysis**: Vocabulary-based sentiment tools rate violence toward animals differently than equivalent violence described with other terms
- **Embedding-based features**: Word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) encode speciesist associations that transfer to downstream classifiers
- **Dataset documentation**: Datasets involving animal-related text or agricultural data may encode speciesist assumptions

## Suggested Change

A brief mention in the fairness/bias documentation sections that speciesist bias is a documented phenomenon in ML, with citations. This helps practitioners consider a broader range of biases when evaluating their models.
author: samtuckerdavis

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
Scikit-learn does not ship pre-trained text embedding or vision models, so I don't think scikit-learn's documentation is the relevant display such a warning.

The TF-IDF transform seems quite neutral by itself, to me. Or at least it will not hide complex word associations the way pre-trained language models can. I don't think that training a text classifier on generic texts from TF-IDF features can silently propagate significant speciesist bias (in particular compared to other harmful biases) from input text to the model decisions unless the choice of the dataset and target variable/classification task themselves are already obviously problematic.

The scikit-learn documentation could probably be improved to mention general research results, evaluation methods and mitigation strategies related to fairness problems and all the kinds of harmful biases that could be unknowingly captured in ML training set and learned models. However, I don't think there is a particular reason to mention literature centered on the particular problem of speciesist biases compared to more general / introductory Ethical ML literature at large.

title: TimeSeries Split: Allow for larger test_size than n_samples // (n_splits + 1)
body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I have a time series y` `with sequence length 1800. Each time stamp is equivalent to 2 seconds, meaning the whole time series covers a time span of 3600 seconds or 1 hour.  
I want to use the first 5 minutes/ 300 seconds/150 time stamps to predict the remaining time series.
Therefore, I want to do a 3-fold time-series cross-validation during the training of the forecasting model. This means that in each split, I take the first 50 time stamps to train the model, and the next 1650 time stamps to validate the model. In the third fold, I then use 150 time stamps (5 minutes) and predict the remaining 1650 time stamps in my series.
When creating the splitter with 
```
splitter = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=3, test_size=int(1800-seq_len))
split = splitter.split(y[0, :])  
```
When looping through the split with
```
for train_index, test_index in split
    train_indexes.append(train_index
    test_indexes.append(test_index) 
```
I get the error:
`ValueError: Too many splits=3 for number of samples=1800 with test_size=1648 and gap=0.`
which is due to the maximum test_size of `n_samples // (n_splits + 1)`.
I wonder why it is not possible to have much larger test sets comparred to train sets?

### Describe your proposed solution

I could, of course, write my own splitter, but I think it would be a good improvement to have this capability also in the `sklearn` framework to make it more complete.
Introducing a gap to only forecast the end of the time series is not an option for me due to the nature of my forecasting algorithm.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_
author: jeiglsperger

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
Thanks for opening this feature request. In general we are not adding a lot of time series specific tooling to scikit-learn and instead recommending to use existing libraries that are compatible with scikit-learn. The reason for this is that time series forecasting is a big field where things are quite different from how most of scikit-learn works (e.g. there is no meaning in the order of samples).

For example https://tscv.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/roll_forward.html looks similar to what you are looking for, but not perfect. Maybe that library is a better place for this than scikit-learn

title: BUG: Trees: minor bug in `NaN` detection leading to incorrect split.
body:
### Describe the bug

The `break` [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/afc095a7b17d5528d62f55f07cab39f963299c78/sklearn/tree/_utils.pyx#L85) is wrong, and in some edge cases it will prevent `_any_isnan_axis0` detecting NaNs for some features. Then because of that, the splitter won't considers splits with NaNs on the left (because it's not aware this feature has NaNs).

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```Python
import numpy as np
from numpy import nan
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

X = np.array([
    [nan, nan],
    [1, 0],
    [1, 1]
])

y = np.array([0, 0, 1])

tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1).fit(X, y)
assert (tree.tree_.impurity[1:] == 0).all()
```

### Expected Results

The best split is found => No assertion error

The best split: `X[:, 1] < 0.5` and missing values to the left node.

Assertion error.

title: PowerTransformer raises raw TypeError on Pandas nullable integer (Int64) and float (Float64) dtypes containing pd.NA
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When passing a Pandas `DataFrame` containing modern nullable extension dtypes (such as `Int64` or `Float64`) with missing values (`pd.NA`) into `PowerTransformer`, the estimator crashes with an unhandled internal exception (`TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`) rather than coercing the array cleanly or raising a standard scikit-learn `ValueError`.

### Context & User-Facing Impact

1. **Modern Pandas Integration:** With modern Pandas workflows (including Pandas 2.0+ defaults and `df.convert_dtypes()`), nullable integer and float types are standard when working with tabular data that contains missing values. 
2. **Pipeline Failures:** In production data pipelines, passing a DataFrame with nullable dtypes directly into a scikit-learn `Pipeline([('power_transform', PowerTransformer()), ...])` causes the entire pipeline to fail with a low-level Pandas boolean evaluation error instead of processing the data smoothly.
3. **Unnecessary Workarounds:** To bypass this bug, users currently have to manually write boilerplate pre-casting logic (e.g., `df.astype("float64")`) before calling `PowerTransformer`, which breaks scikit-learn's native DataFrame compatibility goals.
4. **Consistency:** Most scikit-learn estimators handle Pandas extension arrays seamlessly by converting them to standard floating-point NumPy arrays via `_validate_data`. `PowerTransformer` should follow this same pattern.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

# Minimal DataFrame using Pandas nullable integer extension dtype ('Int64')
# The missing value (None) is automatically represented as pd.NA
X = pd.DataFrame({"col": pd.Series([1, 2, None, 4], dtype="Int64")})

# Triggers raw TypeError inside PowerTransformer during internal array checks
pt = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox")
pt.fit_transform(X)
```

### Expected Results

`PowerTransformer` should automatically coerce Pandas nullable extension arrays into standard IEEE floating-point NumPy arrays (`np.float64` or `np.float32`) via `_validate_data` before evaluating numerical bound checks.

Specifically:
- It should not crash with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`.
- Passing data with nullable dtypes should either complete successfully (coercing `pd.NA` to `np.nan`) or raise a clear, standardized `ValueError` if input constraints are violated.

### Actual Results

The estimator crashes with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous` during internal positivity checks (`X <= 0`):

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "reproduce_bug.py", line 9, in <module>
    pt.fit_transform(X)
  File "sklearn/base.py", line 1478, in fit_transform
    return self.fit(X, **fit_params).transform(X)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3218, in fit
    return self._fit(X, y, force_transform=False)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3232, in _fit
    if np.any(X <= 0):
  File "pandas/core/ops/common.py", line 81, in new_method
    return method(self, other)
TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.3
executable: /usr/bin/python3
   machine: Linux-6.8.0-generic-x86_64

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.0
       pandas: 3.0.4
   matplotlib: 3.9.0
       joblib: 1.4.2
threadpoolctl: 3.5.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in opening a Pull Request to fix this issue once it has been triaged!

### Root Cause Analysis

In `PowerTransformer._fit` (inside `sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py`), positivity and finite bounds checks—such as `np.any(X <= 0)`—are executed on the input `X` **before** array validation occurs:

```python
# Current order of execution in _fit():
if np.any(X <= 0):  # <--- Fails here on Pandas ExtensionArrays containing pd.NA
    raise ValueError(...)

X = self._validate_data(X, ...)

comments.body:
Hi @virchan, thanks for looking into this.

You are correct that the reproducer completes successfully on the main branch.

After further investigation, the issue was specific to an older version of scikit-learn. In the older version, the positivity check (np.any(X <= 0)) was executed before array validation. This caused pd.NA in Pandas ExtensionArrays to trigger the TypeError before it could be coerced.

In the current main branch, the logic has already been refactored (inside _check_input). validate_data is now called first, correctly converting pd.NA into standard np.nan before the numerical bounds check (np.nanmin(X) <= 0) is performed.

Since this is already resolved on main, feel free to close this issue.

A straightforward and low-risk way to address this would be to deduplicate the warning and ensure it is emitted only once.

The deprecation warning itself is valid and originates from a third-party dependency, so suppressing it entirely would not be appropriate. However, repeatedly emitting the same warning during multiprocessing result collection does not add additional value and can be confusing for users.

Emitting a single, contextualized warning would preserve transparency about the underlying issue while avoiding excessive noise, without affecting results or scikit-learn’s public API.

```

### 4. Root cause analysis

This repeated warning is not from `permutation_importance` algorithm itself.

Root cause is in `sklearn.utils.parallel` warning filter propagation:

- scikit-learn sends `warnings.filters` from main process to worker process
- some filter categories are third-party warning classes (example from `pkg_resources`)
- worker unpickle of those class objects can import third-party module again
- import side-effect triggers same deprecation warning many times

So users see repeated warning spam from multiprocessing queue loading.

### 5. Fix solution

I implemented minimal change in `sklearn/utils/parallel.py`:

- before send filters to workers:
  - replace category class object by `(module, qualname)`
- in worker restore stage:
  - resolve category only from `sys.modules` (already-loaded modules)
  - if not loaded / not found, skip this filter

This avoids implicit third-party import at filter restore stage.

import sys

from sklearn.utils.parallel import Parallel, delayed

        "import warnings\\n"

        "class CustomWarning(Warning):\\n"
        "    pass\\n",
        encoding='utf-8',
    )

    sys.path.insert(0, tmp)
    try:
        with warnings.catch_warnings():
            warnings.filterwarnings(

                category=UserWarning,

            mod = __import__('noisywarn')

        with warnings.catch_warnings():
            warnings.simplefilter('ignore', category=mod.CustomWarning)
            Parallel(n_jobs=2, backend='loky')(

title: Segfault in KDTree.query_radius
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

I query a dataset with around 1.6M locations using `KDTree.query_radius`. The script dies in a segfault without an informative error message. 

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Data: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1eAr774HknkcfYFHoOjcic0aY4XetCwUe/view?usp=sharing (⚠️  don't naively `np.load` contents from untrusted source as this can execute arbitrary code on your machine)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import KDTree
import numpy as np

data = np.load("data.npy")

tree = KDTree(data)

query = np.array([
    [651047.8125, 6863169.5]
])

tree.query_radius(query, 800.0, return_distance = True, sort_results = True)
```

### Expected Results

In case there is an issue with the data volumes, there should be at least an informative error message.

### Actual Results

There is a segfault. It works with other query locations, for instance:

comments.author: cakedev0
comments.body:
I see the current code is indeed not guarded against degenerate cases with a O(n) recursion depth (and thus O(n^2) complexity).

Quick recall about quick sort variants:
- 2-way partition: partition the array in `[x < pivot] [x >= pivot]` which is what is currently implemented, or `[x <= pivot] [x >= pivot]` which is what numpy does
- 3-way partition: partition the array in `[x < pivot] [x == pivot] [x > pivot]`. This is very efficient when there are a lot of duplicate values, but otherwise it's less efficient than the 2-way scheme. 

I think that all those schemes can degenerate in O(n^2) complexity for "adversarial" inputs, that's why we usually "guard" them with a heap sort. This mix is called intro sort. For instance, decision trees implement an intro sort with a 3-way partition quick sort.

But for the current partitioning scheme used in `utils/_sorting.pyx` (`[x < pivot] [x >= pivot]`) the adversarial input is as simple as a constant array (or arrays with many duplicates), which is a very common case. So **for now, I propose to simply** change this to the numpy-style partitioning: `[x <= pivot] [x >= pivot]` which doesn't suffer from this problem.

And on the long term, I think it would be nice to share the sorting code with decision trees to have one single file with:
- the heap sort (not used directly, used by other sorts as a fallback)
- a 2-way intro sort: 2-way quick sort with fallback to heap sort when recursion depth degenerates
- a 3-way intro sort: 3-way quick sort with fallback to heap sort when recursion depth degenerates

title: [DOC] Improve docstring for `orthogonal_mp`
body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Currently, the [rendered documentation for `linear_model.orthogonal_mp`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp.html#sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp) ([source](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/cc50648cc1b759b53a4edbce0f3bb6c237349448/sklearn/linear_model/_omp.py#L316-L324)) is missing a formalism and the included LaTeX is not rendered. 

Further, looking at the included formalisms, it seems that the notation is changed between this docstring and [the User Guide section on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html#orthogonal-matching-pursuit-omp), which uses a _w_ rather than a _gamma_.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I see two potential fixes:

1.  Updating the docstring formatting and notation. I would suggest standardizing this with what's currently in the User Guide :

```
    Solves `n_targets` Orthogonal Matching Pursuit problems.
    Each instance of the problem aims to approximate the optimum solution vector, parametrized by the number of non-zero coefficients using
    `n_nonzero_coefs`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||y - Xw||^2_2 \text{subject to} ||w||_0 <= n_{nonzero coefs}

    When parametrized by error using the parameter `tol`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||w||_0 \text{subject to} ||y - Xw||^2_2 <= tol
```

2. Removing this portion of the docstring to direct users towards the formalism in the User Guide, as is done for `linear_model.OrthogonalMatchingPursuit`.

I'm happy to open a PR with either fix !

title: Logic for dtype of `.predict()` from classifiers is inconsistent
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Calling `.predict()` from a classifier may output different dtypes depending on what the input class and dtypes are, in a way that doesn't look consistent.

For example, the [docs for array API support](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/array_api.html) state:
> For estimators, the rule is “everything follows X “ - mixed array inputs are converted so that they all match the array library and device of X.

But that does not appear to be the case with `RidgeClassifier.predict` (currently the only classifier with array API support).

For example, calling `.predict()` with NumPy arrays that are float64 will return int64 under array API dispatch:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"
import numpy as np
import array_api_strict
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(1000, 20))
y = rng.integers(2, size=X.shape[0])

from sklearn import config_context
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
with config_context(array_api_dispatch=True):
    pred = RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(X, y).predict(X)
pred.dtype
```
```
dtype('int64')
```

But with float32 arrays it returns float32, whether it is under array API dispatch or not:
```python
pred = RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(X.astype(np.float32), y.astype(np.float32)).predict(X.astype(np.float32))
pred.dtype
```
```
dtype('float32')
```

Likewise, for pandas it returns the same dtype as input:
```python
import pandas as pd
pred = RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(
    pd.DataFrame(X).astype(np.int16),
    pd.Series(y).astype(np.int16)
).predict(
    pd.DataFrame(X).astype(np.int16)
)
pred.dtype
```
```
dtype('int16')
```

.. unless the input is float64 or mixed types, in which case it returns int64.

But for inputs that are not NumPy, Pandas or Polars, passing float64 will return float64:
```python
import array_api_strict
X64 = array_api_strict.asarray(X, dtype=array_api_strict.float64)
y64 = array_api_strict.asarray(y, dtype=array_api_strict.float64)

with config_context(array_api_dispatch=True):
    pred = RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(X64, y64).predict(X64)
pred.dtype
```
```
array_api_strict.float64
```

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"
import numpy as np
import array_api_strict
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(1000, 20))
y = rng.integers(2, size=X.shape[0])

from sklearn import config_context

title: BUG Spurious UserWarning with the deprecation of penalty in LogisticRegression
body:
When running this minimal example:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(penalty=None).fit(X, y)
```

we get the following deprecation warning:

```
[/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py:1135](http://localhost:8888/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py#line=1134): FutureWarning: 'penalty' was deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10. To avoid this warning, leave 'penalty' set to its default value and use 'l1_ratio' or 'C' instead. Use l1_ratio=0 instead of penalty='l2', l1_ratio=1 instead of penalty='l1', and C=np.inf instead of penalty=None.
```

which is completely fine. In my case, I wanted an unpenalized model and thus fix `C=np.inf`:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf).fit(X, y)
```

and I get the following warning:

```
[/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py:1170](http://localhost:8888/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py#line=1169): UserWarning: Setting penalty=None will ignore the C and l1_ratio parameters
```

I think that this warning is spurious. We probably set the `penalty` internally which trigger this warning.

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
We've had problems downloading data from figshare a few times in the past in the CI. (Probably the same is true for openml?). This makes me think we should try and find a way to rely less on downloaded datasets.

Some ideas for how to do this:
1. mirror the datasets to storage we control/pay for
2. use more synthetic data in our tests
3. use a small number of datasets (one or two?) for all of our tests
4. run a proxy that caches the datasets for a very long/infinite time 

I numbered the options I could think of to make it easier to refer to them, not as an indication of preference.

I don't like the idea of mirroring the datasets. They will eventually become out of sync or other "wonderfully weird" things will happen. However it is pragmatic because these "weird changes" will probably happen less often than access issues.

I think (2) might be doable for the tests, but I think our examples would be a lot less good if they used synthetic data only. At least the easy to generate datasets are very abstract (I find).

Not sure if (3) would help us in the current case. But it might reduce the load on dataset hosts, which frees up time/resources to work on other things that will make them even more reliable.

Option (4) is probably easy on day one and day two. We could cache things for a very long time and empty the cache whenever we need to have the cached version refreshed. A tricky thing is that people will discover that we have this proxy and will start using it. So we would need some kind of authentication layer. And now this starts to be a bigger project already.

So overall, no great options? I'm kinda excited about (4) but that is the technologist in me talking, not the person who can predict 5 months into the future. What other ideas are there?

Based on

and

This solution together with local cache and checksum checks (local, figshare, and OpenML have metadata containing the checksum) should be quite reliable.

title: AttributeError: cross_val_predict(method='predict_proba') with MultiOutputClassifier (swev-id: scikit-learn__scikit-learn-14629)
body:
## User Request

AttributeError with `cross_val_predict(method='predict_proba')` when using `MultiOutputClassifier`.

Description:
Using `cross_val_predict(method='predict_proba')` with `MultiOutputClassifier` triggers `AttributeError` because `estimator.classes_` is accessed; `MultiOutputClassifier` exposes `classes_` per sub-estimator as `estimators_[i].classes_`. Proposed fix: store `classes_` at the wrapper level like `ClassifierChain` does, and adjust validation code paths.

Repro:
```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_multilabel_classification
from sklearn.multioutput import MultiOutputClassifier
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
X, Y = make_multilabel_classification()
mo_lda = MultiOutputClassifier(LinearDiscriminantAnalysis())
pred = cross_val_predict(mo_lda, X, Y, cv=5)  # Works
pred_proba = cross_val_predict(mo_lda, X, Y, cv=5, method='predict_proba')  # Error
```

Observed failure (branch: `scikit-learn__scikit-learn-14629`):
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 8, in <module>
  File "sklearn/model_selection/_validation.py", line 625, in cross_val_predict
    # ... setup omitted ...
  File "sklearn/model_selection/_validation.py", line 859, in _fit_and_predict
    predictions = [_enforce_prediction_order(
        estimator.classes_[i_label], predictions[i_label],
        n_classes=len(set(y[:, i_label])), method=method)
    for i_label in range(len(predictions))]
AttributeError: 'MultiOutputClassifier' object has no attribute 'classes_'
```

## Researcher Specification

- cross_val_predict handling for `method='predict_proba'` enforces class order via `_enforce_prediction_order`, expecting a top-level `estimator.classes_` that is indexable per output when predictions is a list.
- In this branch, `_validation.py` does:
  ```python
  predictions = [_enforce_prediction_order(
      estimator.classes_[i_label], predictions[i_label],
      n_classes=len(set(y[:, i_label])), method=method)
      for i_label in range(len(predictions))]
  ```
  which requires `estimator.classes_` at the wrapper level.
- `MultiOutputClassifier` (in `sklearn/multioutput.py`) currently does not define `self.classes_` at the wrapper level after `fit`. Each underlying estimator has its own `.classes_`.
- `ClassifierChain` in the same module sets `self.classes_ = [estimator.classes_ for estimator in self.estimators_]` during `fit`.

### Proposed Fix
- Modify `MultiOutputClassifier` to set a wrapper-level `classes_` after `fit` (and update on `partial_fit` if applicable), mirroring `ClassifierChain`:
  - In `sklearn/multioutput.py`, within `class MultiOutputClassifier`:
    - Add to Attributes docstring:
      - `classes_ : list` — list of length `n_outputs`; each element is an array of class labels for the corresponding output.
    - Implement:
      ```python
      def fit(self, X, y, sample_weight=None):
          super().fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight)
          self.classes_ = [estimator.classes_ for estimator in self.estimators_]
          return self
      ```
    - Optionally:
      ```python
      @if_delegate_has_method('estimator')
      def partial_fit(self, X, y, classes=None, sample_weight=None):
          super().partial_fit(X, y, classes=classes, sample_weight=sample_weight)
          if all(hasattr(e, 'classes_') for e in self.estimators_):
              self.classes_ = [e.classes_ for e in self.estimators_]
          return self
      ```
- No changes needed in `cross_val_predict` validation: it already handles list predictions and expects `wrapper.classes_[i]`.

### Tests
- Add regression tests (e.g., in `sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_validation.py`):
  1) LDA + `MultiOutputClassifier` with `cross_val_predict(method='predict_proba')` should return a list of length `n_outputs`; each array shape `(n_samples, n_classes_i)` with rows summing to 1.
  2) Mixed binary/multiclass outputs (e.g., `LogisticRegression` base) maintain correct shapes and order.
  3) `cross_val_predict` without `method` remains working for multi-output classifiers.

### Risks/Notes
- If any sub-estimator lacks `predict_proba`, `MultiOutputClassifier.predict_proba` raises `ValueError`; `cross_val_predict(method='predict_proba')` will propagate accordingly.
- Class order differences across folds are handled by `_enforce_prediction_order` (existing behavior).
- Multi-output with different class sets per target is represented naturally by list-of-arrays `classes_`.

We will implement this fix on a dedicated branch and open a single PR targeting `scikit-learn__scikit-learn-14629`.

title: DOC: Improve formula explanation and add table for train/test sizes in TimeSeriesSplit
body:
Hi @scikit-learn/core-devs,

I created this documentation improvement for `TimeSeriesSplit` because the current formula in the Notes section is quite hard to understand for many users.

I have read the [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), especially the section for new contributors.

I would like to work on this myself once it is triaged and approved. Is this issue suitable for a first-time contributor?

Thank you!
author: anikchand461

comments.author: anikchand461
comments.body:
### Current Problem

In `TimeSeriesSplit` (`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py`), the Notes section contains this formula:

> The training set has size ``i * n_samples // (n_splits + 1) + n_samples % (n_splits + 1)`` in the ``i`` th split,  
> with a test set of size ``n_samples//(n_splits + 1)`` by default...

This formula is difficult for many users (especially beginners) to understand quickly. There is no visual aid or simple table showing how train and test sizes change across folds when using different combinations of `n_splits`, `test_size`, and `gap`.

The current examples show code output but do not clearly demonstrate the practical effect of these parameters.

### Why it matters
Many users get confused about:
- How the training set grows across successive folds
- The combined effect of `test_size` and `gap`
- When and why to use `max_train_size`

This makes one of the most important time-series cross-validation tools harder to use than necessary.

### Proposed Improvement

- Replace or supplement the formula with a clean markdown table showing train/test sizes for common cases.
- Add a simple plain-English explanation before the table.
- Mention a real-world use case (e.g., preventing data leakage in forecasting).

**Location**: `sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` → `class TimeSeriesSplit` (Notes section)

I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this documentation improvement myself once the issue is triaged and approved.

title: TST: Add edge-case tests for StratifiedGroupKFold
body:
### Current Problem

`StratifiedGroupKFold` has complex logic in `_iter_test_indices` and `_find_best_fold`. 
There are several corner cases (e.g. groups with only one sample, very uneven class distributions, or small number of groups) that can lead to unexpected behavior or degenerate splits.

Current test coverage for these edge cases is limited.

### Proposed Improvement

Add targeted tests in `sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_split.py` for:

- Each group containing only one sample
- One class appearing in only one group
- `shuffle=True` with a small number of groups
- Cases where `n_splits` is close to the number of groups

This will help prevent regressions and increase confidence in the implementation.

**Location**:  
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` (class `StratifiedGroupKFold`) + corresponding tests in `test_split.py`

I have already opened a few documentation issues. I would like to work on adding these tests once this issue is triaged.

title: [BUG] MinMaxScaler fails with JAX arrays due to in-place assignment in _handle_zeros_in_scale
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using MinMaxScaler with the experimental Array API dispatching enabled, passing a JAX array causes a TypeError. This happens because internal helper functions (specifically _handle_zeros_in_scale) attempt in-place item assignment (scale[mask] = 1.0), which is not supported by JAX's immutable arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"
import jax.numpy as jnp
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler
from sklearn import set_config

set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

data = jnp.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]], dtype=jnp.float32)
scaler = MinMaxScaler(copy=True)
transformed_data = scaler.fit_transform(data)

### Expected Results

No Error is thrown

### Actual Results

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in working on a PR to resolve this once it has been triaged.

The root cause is a violation of the "functional" requirement of the Array API specification within the _handle_zeros_in_scale helper function in sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py.

The current implementation uses in-place item assignment:

scale[constant_mask] = 1.0

While this works for mutable backends like NumPy, it triggers a TypeError for immutable backends like JAX.
The fix involves moving from a mutating assignment to a functional selection. I propose using xp.where from the Array API namespace. This is backend-agnostic and works across NumPy, JAX, and PyTorch.

comments.author: virchan
comments.body:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to scikit-learn, @MuhammadEssa2002.

scikit-learn’s array API support does not currently include `jax.numpy` (see the [array API support page](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/array_api.html) and https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/29647 for context).

Regarding the `TypeError`, the underlying cause goes beyond the root cause you identified. JAX does not support in-place updates, see also https://github.com/data-apis/array-api/issues/609 for additional context.

With that said, I'm closing this issue.

title: `propagate_callback_context` checks a public method but calls a private one
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

In `sklearn/callback/_callback_context.py` the `CallbackContext.propagate_callback_context` method checks the public name while the call uses the private one (`_set_callbacks()`). This is the result of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34096 which is where I think the private method was introduced.

```python
if callbacks_to_propagate and not hasattr(sub_estimator, "set_callbacks"):
    ...  # warn "does not support callbacks" and skip propagation

if callbacks_to_propagate:
    curr_callbacks = getattr(sub_estimator, "_skl_callbacks", [])
    # Now uses _set_callbacks
    sub_estimator._set_callbacks(curr_callbacks + callbacks_to_propagate)
```

Is it a requirement to support the private method as well if you want to implement an estimator with callback support? Or is the `if` statement a leftover from before?

I grepped for `set_callbacks` in `doc/developers/callback_support.rst` but couldn't find a mention of the private version
author: betatim

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
A few more minutes of code reading lead me to realise that you have to inherit from `CallbackSupportMixin` (so say the docs), so I think this means for a third party estimator that wants to support callbacks this is also a requirement. If you inherit from it then you gain the private method "for free".

So I think I'll close this because the answer to my question is that I found this problem in the context of an estimator that doesn't inherit, which is "the bug".
