comments.body:
> I have done local tests that seem to work. If I am missing something about the purpose of multiple CSS blocks, I would love to know.

I am not sure I understand what changed. Can you open a draft PR so that we can see the diff?

comments.author: DeaMariaLeon
comments.body:
I mean that we could add the `<style></style>` blocks only once with `estimator.py`. I didn't mean in the header section. My main point was that I fail to see the purpose of the dynamic selectors on `estimator.css`. If that isn't needed, the file can be loaded only once if we use a cache. 

I'll open a draft PR, it will be easier.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
> I mean that we could add the <style></style> blocks only once with estimator.py.

But how does scikit-learn can know that a previous call to `estimator_html_repr` has already been included in a user facing DOM tree or not?

There might be a single Python program that executes several notebook files (e.g. `nbconvert`) and it's hard to know whether individual calls to `estimator_html_repr` are redundant or not.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
The fundamental problem is that `estimator_html_repr` does not have access to inspect the to target HTML document: it cannot know if other estimators HTML snippets have already been included in the target HTML doc or not.

EDIT: furthermore, when we run interactive Python code with Jupyter notebooks or VS Code, the Python code is executed within an ipykernel process. As far as I know, this Python process has no awareness on whether its output will be included in an HTML document object tree or not and if several consecutive cell executions stem from the same HTML document object tree or from several independent documents. I think the designers of the Jupyter kernel protocol decided to make the kernel execution completely decoupled from the rendering of the previously executed cells by design. I think this is a fundamental limitation of the jupyter protocol.

comments.author: DeaMariaLeon
comments.body:
OK, but if the css rules don't change for each estimator, maybe we don't need a dynamic selector. At least getting rid of the Template and substitution may improve a bit? Opened a draft PR.

For the rest - the repeated <style></style> I was overlooking stuff. I was thinking that I could use `lru_cache` for example, not reading from HTML. But I guess not.

Just to be clear: I do understand the need of several styling blocks. 
My PR only touches CSS logic.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Bin creation is a surprisingly large chunk of at least some of the histogram gradient boosting benchmarks; a big chunk of that is `np.argsort()`. I am fairly certain it can be faster, e.g. full sorting is probably unnecessary in many cases.

### Describe your proposed solution

Current ideas (perhaps all wrong!) that I expect to try:
 
* A quick experiment suggests `np.argpartition` is way faster than `np.argsort` and plausibly viable in some common cases. I _think_ even that may be overkill.
* It would not surprise me if the unique values calculation is unnecessary on the full data, and running it just on the bins might suffice.
* Maybe NumPy's own histogram calculation might work sometimes?

Etc. Still TBD if any of this is actually correct.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

I will try to implement some of these, and if I succeed then submit a PR.

title: Mixed string/numeric when input is list for classification metrics
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This is not a good first (or second) issue to contribute. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn please have a look at our [contributing doc](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html) and in particular the section [Issues for new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors). 

Noticed while working on #32755

Classification metrics (`CLASSIFICATION_METRICS` from `test_common.py`, they are all defined in `sklearn/metrics/_classification.py`, but not all metrics in `_classification.py` fall in this list) vary in how they handle mixed string and numeric inputs (e.g., `y_true` is string and `y_pred` is numeric).

* `precision_recall_fscore_support` and friends (`precision_score`, `recall_score`, `f1_score`, `fbeta_score` and related `jaccard_score`) - raises `ValueError`:
   * via `_check_set_wise_labels`, which calls [`unique_labels`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/66200f149ba6c64a3a93dd73e37bdeea87bb5db8/sklearn/utils/multiclass.py#L41), which does not allow "mix of string and integer labels“
   * note that these metrics do take a `pos_label` parameter, so theoretically when `y_true` is string, we could use `y_true == pos_label` to convert to [1,0]. This would not make sense if `y_pred` was string.
* `confusion_matrix` (and metrics that use it - `balanced_accuracy_score`, `cohen_kappa_score`) - raises `ValueError` ONLY when `labels=None`:
   * `labels=None`: calls [`unique_labels`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/66200f149ba6c64a3a93dd73e37bdeea87bb5db8/sklearn/utils/multiclass.py#L41) like above
   * `labels` is set - AFAICT no error but the confusion matrix would only contain 0. e.g., if `y_true` is string and `labels` is set to all possible unique values in `y_true`, we would do the following conversion:
  
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/66200f149ba6c64a3a93dd73e37bdeea87bb5db8/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py#L584-L587

Since none of the string `labels` are present in numeric `y_pred`, `y_pred` would be converted to array that consists only of `n_labels + 1` values

* `multilabel_confusion_matrix` - always raises raises `ValueError` (again via `unique_labels`):
   * unlike `confusion_matrix`, even when `labels` is given, we call `unique_labels(y_true, y_pred)` to get all labels present, and if any are not provided in `labels` they are added.

The following all DO NOT error:

* `accuracy_score` - no error but result would always be 0 (as `score = y_true == y_pred` would always be 0). Note not relevant for multilabel cases as input needs to be label indicator matrix.
* `hamming_loss` - no error but result would always be 1. Again not relevant for multilabel.
* `zero_one_loss` - no error but result would always be 1 (when `normalize=False`). Again not relevant for multilabel.
* `matthews_corrcoef` - no error but result would always be 0. Note that we transform `y_true` and `y_pred` using `LabelEncoder` fit on `y_true` and `y_pred` concat (meaning `y_true` and `y_pred` will be numbers, but not contain any numbers in common), before we pass to `confusion_matrix`.

For these classification metrics which require `y_pred` to be thresholded predictions, I don't think it makes sense to have mixed string and numeri (e.g., how would you match ['apple', 'orange', 'apple] to [2,3,2] ?). Indeed, for the metrics that do not error, the result is the 'worst' value.
For metrics that accept `pos_label` the way forward is less clear. Note that for several continuous classification metrics we do use something like `y_true == pos_label`, thus allowing `y_true` to be string.

Note that I will open a separate issue around this for continuous classification metrics (i.e. those in `_ranking.py`).

cc @ogrisel
author: lucyleeow

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
I don't think we need thresholded/hard classification metrics to support mixed string/numeric inputs. The classification labels and the hard class predictions should always use the same type of values (either string or integers). All the metrics derived from confusion matrix fall into that case.

But we do need mixed inputs for unthresholded/soft classification metrics such as log loss, Brier score, ROC AUC, Average Precision... Basically any metric that accepts a mix of true string/integer label along with continuous predicteds scores.

comments.author: lucyleeow
comments.body:
I've realised there was a bad typo above, which I just fixed. The last 4 metrics do not error.

So for the 4 metrics that do not currently error, we should amend them to make them error? (and also amend `multilabel_confusion_matrix` such that it always errors)

Edit: Just checked the continuous classification metrics and they all have consistent behaviour, I had thought they'd be a mixed bag like the classification metrics

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: I think the thresholded metrics should raise an error if passed inconsistent types of inputs.

comments.author: lucyleeow
comments.body:
I've just realised the lack of error for inconsistent types is only for lists (and non-object type numpy arrays), we actually handle array inputs fine (#18192):

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/6c084a8152d41419fb7baf2bc1692890385d6599/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py#L154-L165


(`_union1d` will not raise an error for mixed str and number types when input is list)

I will work on fixing this for lists and updating the test.

title: StratifiedGroupKFold produces empty / degenerate splits
body:
### Describe the bug

StratifiedGroupKFold seems to be broken (Python 3.13, scikit-learn 1.8.0) for some fairly simple grouped classification datasets, quite frequently producing empty training or test sets. 

While I am aware of the many issues covering poor stratification and the workarounds suggested (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/24656, https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/12076), this is a much more annoying problem in automated pipelines, as we can't even assume that e.g. 5-fold actually produces 5 valid folds. 

This seems not to be some rare example, but occurs very often with some pretty simple grouped classification datasets, even when the number of samples is quite large (see attached script `demo.py`).

I really hope I am not doing something dumb here, because this seems to be a pretty big issue otherwise. I think the issue is that, obviously, when the number of groups and/or labels is small, and when these are not both distributed uniformly and independently over the samples, then it can just be the case that you simply cannot satisfy all three goals of balanced folds, groups, and target / y labels simultaneously in a satisfactory way. However, in such cases, there should surely be a warning and some kind of natural fallback (perhaps not stratifying, or ignoring grouping, depending on an option), or perhaps an error. 

But producing a degenerate fold definitely does not feel right. 

[demo.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24630346/demo.py)

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold

y = [0, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
g = [0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1]
skf = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=False)

for fold, (ix_train, ix_test) in enumerate(skf.split(X=y, y=y, groups=g)):
    if len(ix_train) == 0:
        assert len(ix_test) == len(y)
        degen = "training"
    elif len(ix_test) == 0:
        assert len(ix_train) == len(y)
        degen = "test"
    else:
        continue

    print(f"Degenerate (empty) {degen} set on fold {fold + 1} for data:")
    print(f"y = {y}")
    print(f"g = {g}")
```

### Expected Results

We should not be getting empty training or test sets with any k-fold method. This will almost always cause errors downstream. 

### Actual Results

If you run `demo.py`, you will see a large number of combinations of grouping variables and classification targets cause degenerate splits.

### Versions

```shell
>>> import sklearn
>>> sklearn.show_versions()

System:
    python: 3.13.9 (main, Oct 14 2025, 21:10:40) [Clang 20.1.4 ]
executable: /Users/me/Documents/groupkfold/.venv/bin/python
   machine: macOS-15.5-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.8.0
          pip: None
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.4.1
        scipy: 1.17.0
       Cython: None
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Built with OpenMP: True

threadpoolctl info:
       user_api: openmp
   internal_api: openmp
    num_threads: 8
         prefix: libomp
       filepath: /Users/me/Documents/groupkfold/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/sklearn/.dylibs/libomp.dylib
        version: None
```
author: DM-Berger

comments.author: sun-9545sunoj
comments.body: Hi @DM-Berger , I am interested in working on this issue. I have reproduced the bug using the provided script and would like to be assigned to it.

comments.author: AnneBeyer
comments.body: Hi @sun-9545sunoj thank you for your interest, but please check [Issues tagged “Needs Triage”](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) and wait until consensus has been reached on how to handle this issue.

comments.author: sun-9545sunoj
comments.body: Thanks for the clarification! I’ll keep an eye on the discussion and would be happy to help once a direction is agreed upon.

comments.author: DM-Berger
comments.body:
So, from some further testing, it seems mostly this issue boils down to the current implementation failing to check for the case where the number of groups, $g$ is less than the number of folds, $k$. IMO this is a simple degenerate case where grouped splitting is impossible, and so this should be checked and simply raise a ValueError. 

The current implementation instead silently produces degenerate splits. If raising an exception is unpalatable, then IMO at bare minimum, the documentation should be updated to note that invoking StratifiedGroupKFold with less groups than folds puts you in the realm of undefined behaviour, i.e. this is a case that is not properly handled, and which has no intention of being properly handled. 

But right now, without a warning, error, or documentation, it is surprisingly easy for the current behaviour to cause hard-to-detect bugs in more complex automated pipelines.

EDIT: I might also add, if you are in the case where $g < k$, then, since in practice one rarely chooses anything other than 3, 5, or 10 for $k$, a viable alternative validation in many of these cases will be LeaveOneGroupOut validation. This might be useful to include in an error message and/or warning and/or documentation.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
I agree with your assessment @DM-Berger.

I checked an `GroupKFold` raises an exception in that case:

```
ValueError: Cannot have number of splits n_splits=3 greater than the number of groups: 2.
```

I think we should align the behavior of the two splitters. @DM-Berger would you be interested in opening a PR or would rather have someone else fix this bug?

comments.author: DM-Berger
comments.body: Yes @ogrisel, if anyone else wants to open a PR to resolve this, that's great, I don't have the bandwidth for this currently. Raising a `ValueError` like `GroupKFold` seems the simplest and most sensible approach to me as well.

comments.author: akshath-raj
comments.body:
Cross-linking: #34828 reports another cause of the empty folds described here, independent of the `n_groups < n_splits` case that #33176 addressed.

`_find_best_fold` compares fold scores with an exact `<` before its `np.isclose` tiebreak, so a 1-ULP difference between mathematically tied scores can send a group to a fold that already holds one and leave another fold empty. This still happens when `n_groups == n_splits`:

```python
y = [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0]
g = [0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 3, 3, 0, 2]
# StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=4) -> test fold sizes [5, 8, 0, 5]
```

Flagging it here since it bears on whether this issue is fully resolved. Details and measurements are in #34828.

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
The issue discussed here was resolved in #33176 by alligning the behaviours of  `StratifiedGroupKFold` and `GroupKFold` so that the former throws a `ValueError` like the latter.

I will therefore close this issue as completed.

title: `cross_validate` slows down with `n_jobs > 1`
body:

The time needed to`cross_validate` can have a big (x100) slow down when using parallel jobs (`n_jobs > 1`).

The docstring for `ExtraTree*.fit` is the same than the one of `DecisionTree*` so it's inaccurate:

> Build a decision tree regressor from the training set (X, y).

> Return:
>     self : DecisionTreeRegressor
>        Fitted estimator.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Removing `ExtraTree*` classes would fix this (this is one option considered in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/33158)

Otherwise we need to add a fit method to those classes.

Bean Labs took a source pass. In `sklearn/tree/_classes.py`, `ExtraTreeClassifier` inherits from `DecisionTreeClassifier` and `ExtraTreeRegressor` inherits from `DecisionTreeRegressor`; the parent classes define the `fit(...)` docstrings that mention building a decision tree.

A small docs fix would be to override the generated/public `fit` doc text for the ExtraTree classes while leaving the inherited implementation alone. A regression could inspect the rendered estimator docs or generated docstring for `ExtraTreeClassifier.fit` and `ExtraTreeRegressor.fit` so the inherited wording does not come back.

No PR opened from this pass.

The ExtraTree* estimator classes inherit their fit method docstring from DecisionTree* base classes. The fit parameters are identical, so using the parent docstring is correct behavior. This is not a bug but an intentional reuse via inheritance.

The docstrings are inherited through the standard class hierarchy and reflect the actual parameter signatures accurately. No change needed.

title: Fitted attribute display can be misleading because of the default rounding
body: ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact For instance, if you have a small value (such as 1e-6, 1e-12), it is displayed as 0. In some cases it can be misleading because you know that this value is expected to be non-zero as in the following cases: ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV import numpy as np rng = np.random.RandomState(0) y = rng.randn(100) X = y[:, None] alphas = np.logspace(-12, 12, 13) regressor = RidgeCV(alphas=alphas).fit(X, y) regressor ``` The displayed value for `alpha_` is surprising because we know that it's supposed to belong to one of the `alphas` passed as argument: ```python >>> alphas array([1.e-12, 1.e-10, 1.e-08, 1.e-06, 1.e-04, 1.e-02, 1.e+00, 1.e+02, 1.e+04, 1.e+06, 1.e+08, 1.e+10, 1.e+12]) ``` And if you look at the fitted attribute interactively, it's rendered "correctly" by jupyter/IPython: ```python >>> regressor.alpha_ 1e-12 ``` ### Expected Results The HTML display should use an alternative string representation for float attributes with a less misleading way of rounding, for instance '1e-12' as rendered by the following formatting string that should use 4 numerical digits using the scientific notation: ```python >>> f"{regressor.alpha_:.4g}" '1e-12' ``` or: ```python >>> f"{regressor.alpha_:.4e}" '1.0000e-12' ``` ### Actual Results See the rendered HTML table above. ### Versions ```shell Today's `main` branch (1.9.dev0). ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug I don't want to fix the bug myself if @DeaMariaLeon is interested in working on a PR for this.

So it does seem like a variation of the cython 3.2.6 regression https://github.com/cython/cython/issues/7767 with a `pickle` `dumps/loads` roundtrip on top of it? cc @da-woods for expert advice on whether this can be considered a Cython bug or not (it kind of seems like one).

I created a minimal reproducer in https://github.com/lesteve/scikit-learn-34525-cython-reproducer.


My understanding is that using `functools.update_wrapper` on a Cython function will fail the `pickle` `dumps/loads` roundtrip with the confusing error `AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute '__annotate__'`.

Here is an example closer to the scikit-learn code:

```py
import pickle
from functools import update_wrapper

import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KDTree


class Wrapper:
    def __init__(self, function):
        self.function = function
        # if you remove the next line this works
        update_wrapper(self, function)

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        return self.function(*args, **kwargs)


tree = KDTree(np.zeros((2, 2)))
wrapped = Wrapper(tree.query)

payload = pickle.dumps(wrapped)
# The next line yields AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute '__annotate__'
pickle.loads(payload)
```

title: Degraded performance of `enet_path` due to #31882
body:
### Describe the bug

I need to use a significantly tighter value of `tol` to get the same quality of convergence from `enet_path` since #31882.

The point of running `enet_path` with a large number of alphas $\alpha_1 > \cdots > \alpha_n$  is that the resulting betas $\beta_1, \cdots, \beta_n$ are very close together, hence $\beta_k$ is a good initial guess for $\beta_{k+1}$.

In the example below, I expect to get 100 different betas, but I get just 20. The new code doesn't update beta at each step. It waits until beta becomes a "bad guess" for the next beta. Doesn't seem like a helpful optimization.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import enet_path


def main():
    height = 10_000
    width = 10

    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    X = rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=(height, width))
    beta_true = rng.uniform(-100, 100, size=width)
    y = X @ beta_true

    _alphas, coefs, _dual_gaps = enet_path(X, y, eps=1e-9, l1_ratio=1.0)  # type: ignore

    u = np.unique(coefs, axis=1)
    n_unique_coefs = u.shape[1]
    print(n_unique_coefs)

    diff = beta_true - coefs[:, -1]
    diffnorm = np.linalg.norm(diff)
    print(diffnorm)
```

### Expected Results

1.7.2:
```
100
2.8294111246854234e-07
```

### Actual Results

1.8.0:
```
20
0.43002957697539734
```

comments.author: PHclaw
comments.body:
For the LogisticRegressionCV with use_legacy_attributes=False and refit=False:

The crash happens because `use_legacy_attributes=False` changes the internal attribute names, but `refit=False` path still references the old names. Fix:

```python
# In LogisticRegressionCV.refit()
if self.use_legacy_attributes:
    self.coef_ = best_coefs
    self.intercept_ = best_intercepts
else:
    self.coefficients_ = best_coefs
    self.intercepts_ = best_intercepts
```

The `refit=False` code path needs the same dual-path logic.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: I confirm I can reproduce the bug.

comments.author: Fazel94
comments.body:
In the `refit=False` branch, the code stored `None` into `self.l1_ratio_` for
non-elasticnet penalties, using it as a "not applicable" sentinel.  
Later, the
`use_legacy_attributes=False` block unconditionally called `float(self.l1_ratio_[0])`, which
fails on `None`.  

To fix I replaced None with 0.0 for any non-elasticnet penalty, `l1_ratio` is semantically irrelevant, 0.0 is the correct placeholder pure L2, consistent with what the `refit=True` code path already stored in equivalent situation.

comments.author: ishanvaibhav
comments.body:
I was able to reproduce this issue locally using the provided example.

I also tested the fix in #33902, and it resolves the TypeError on my end. The explanation regarding `l1_ratio_` being set to `None` in the `refit=False` path and later cast to float makes sense.

Using `0.0` as a placeholder for non-elasticnet penalties seems consistent with the `refit=True` behavior and avoids the crash.

It might be helpful to add a regression test for this configuration (`refit=False`, `use_legacy_attributes=False`, non-elasticnet solver) to ensure this edge case is covered going forward.

Thanks for working on this!

title: DOC/ENH: StandardScaler silently sets scale to 1.0 for zero-variance features with no warning
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a recent CS/AI graduate currently building a personal finance app that uses scikit-learn for some ML-based features (budgeting insights, basic predictive modeling). While setting up a local editable build to start learning the codebase and look for ways to contribute, I was testing edge cases with StandardScaler and noticed it silently returns a scale of 1.0 for zero-variance features (e.g. a single-sample fit) without any warning or documentation of this behavior. I dug into the source (_handle_zeros_in_scale) to confirm it was intentional rather than a bug, and found the public docstring doesn't mention it.

I'd like to help fix this if it's something the maintainers agree is worth addressing — happy to work on either a documentation update or a warning, whichever direction you'd prefer.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

StandardScaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or
warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample
fit, or a constant column. This is implemented via the internal
_handle_zeros_in_scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the
public StandardScaler docstring or the User Guide.

Minimal reproduction:

​```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3]])  # single sample — zero variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
# Output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised
​```

This could silently mask real data problems — e.g. an accidental single-row
fit, or a constant column slipping through a preprocessing pipeline —
producing all-zero output with no signal to the user that something
unusual happened.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Adding a note to the StandardScaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the User Guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale_ is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than NaN or inf. This would at least make the existing behavior discoverable without changing any code.
author: RoboDevelopX

comments.author: Seif-Elkerdany
comments.body:
I took a look at this on the current `main` branch.

It looks like the exact zero-variance behavior is already documented in the public `StandardScaler` docstring under `scale_`:

> “If a variance is zero, we can't achieve unit variance, and the data is left as-is, giving a scaling factor of 1.”

The behavior also appears to be intentional and explicitly tested for constant features in `sklearn/preprocessing/tests/test_data.py`.

One small distinction is that `scale_ = 1` does not necessarily mean that the transformed feature is all zeros. With the default `with_mean=True`, a constant feature becomes zero because it is first centered and then divided by 1. With `with_mean=False`, the constant feature instead passes through unchanged.

For example:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X = np.array([[5.0], [5.0], [5.0]])

scaler = StandardScaler(with_mean=False)
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
print(scaler.scale_)
```
gives a scale of 1 while the values remain 5.

I also found #19547, which already tracks the broader question of whether `StandardScaler` and other estimators should warn when fitted on constant features. The discussion there also mentions the risk of generating many warnings in pipelines and cross-validation.

There may still be a narrower documentation question here for *near-constant* features. `StandardScaler` uses `_is_constant_feature` to identify features whose variance is numerically indistinguishable from zero, and `_handle_zeros_in_scale` sets their scale to 1 for numerical stability. The public `scale_` documentation currently describes the exact zero-variance case, but does not seem to explain this near-constant/numerical-stability case explicitly.

So perhaps this issue could be narrowed to whether that near-constant behavior should be documented more explicitly, while the warning discussion remains in #19547.

comments.author: sejal04-hash
comments.body:
Hi, thanks for the clarification.

I understand that the exact zero-variance behavior is already documented and tested, and that the warning discussion is covered by #19547.

Would it be appropriate to narrow this issue to documenting the near-zero variance / numerical-stability behavior of `StandardScaler` more explicitly in the `scale_` documentation or User Guide?

If so, I would be happy to work on the documentation update.

comments.author: AnneBeyer
comments.body: Hi @RoboDevelopX, thank you for wanting to contribute, but given the context from @Seif-Elkerdany's comment (thank you, that was super helpful!!!) that this is actually documented and tested behavior (thus not silent) and that the warning part is being discussed in another issue, I'll close this one. Extending the docstring to include the case where the variance is not zero but "numerically indistinguishable from zero" is not a priority, as we have too many other open things that require maintainer attention.

title: Redundant execution of  check_class_weight_balanced_linear_classifier
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In sklearn/utils/estimator_checks.py, the function _yield_classifier_checks yields check_class_weight_balanced_linear_classifier twice for linear classifiers that support the class_weight parameter.

This bug was discovered during a manual code review of estimator_checks.py. It affects any scikit-learn user or developer who uses check_estimator (or the underlying check generators) to validate estimators.

The impact is redundant test execution. For example, when running common tests for a LogisticRegression or a custom linear classifier using the mixin, this specific check (which involves fitting the estimator and verifying class weight handling) is executed twice. This is wasteful in terms of CI/CD time and can lead to duplicated error messages or logs, making debugging more tedious.



### Steps/Code to Reproduce

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import _yield_classifier_checks
def get_name(check):
    return getattr(check, "__name__",
                   getattr(check, "func", check).__name__)
clf = LogisticRegression()
checks = list(_yield_classifier_checks(clf))
check_names = [get_name(c) for c in checks]
duplicate_count = check_names.count(
    'check_class_weight_balanced_linear_classifier'
)
print(f"Yield count: {duplicate_count}")

### Expected Results

The check should be yielded exactly once. Yield count: 1

### Actual Results

The check is currently yielded twice. Yield count: 2

### Versions

```shell
python: 3.14.0
numpy: 2.4.1
scipy: 1.17.0
joblib: 1.5.3
scikit-learn: 1.7.dev0 (from source)
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

I am interested in fixing this bug. I have already identified the root cause and implemented a fix.

Analysis of root cause: In _yield_classifier_checks, there are two consecutive if blocks that both check for isinstance(classifier, LinearClassifierMixin) and the presence of class_weight in parameters. Both blocks yield the same check.

comments.body:
It seems that SciPy performed changes which alter the interfaces for BLAS.

Accepting this new version of SciPy would break forward-compatibility (previous builds of scikit-learn won't be compatible with new builds of SciPy) and backward-compatibility (builds of scikit-learn built against the new version of SciPy won't be compatible with previous build of SciPy).

IMO, the best pathway is to revert the changes in SciPy for now and see whether the newly introduced interfaces for BLAS could come as additions rather than as replacements.

comments.author: morikaransinh
comments.body:
hey @sakaiando 
LassoCV and ElasticNetCV expect y to be a 1D array because they do not support multi-output regression. When a 2D column vector is passed, sklearn flattens it internally and raises a warning to ensure the user is aware of this implicit conversion.

why :

Ridge supports multiple outputs because its L2 penalty leads to a smooth, convex objective with a closed-form matrix solution. Lasso uses an L1 penalty, which introduces non-differentiability and requires coordinate descent. Extending this efficiently and stably to multi-output cross-validated settings is complex, so scikit-learn restricts LassoCV and ElasticNetCV to single-output regression and provides MultiTaskLasso variants instead.

title: RFC change default `scoring` of `LogisticRegressionCV` from  accuracy to logloss
body:
I propose to change the default value of `LogisticRegressionCV(scoring=None)` (`None` uses accuracy) to `LogisticRegressionCV(scoring=neg_log_loss)`.

Reason:
- Logistic Regression minimizes (penalized) log loss when fitting.
- Scoring with accuracy calls `LogisticRegression.predict` which applies an arbitrary probability threshold of 50%.
- Because of the 50% threshold, it happens that parameters with the same accuracy but better log loss (=better probability predictions) don't get selected.
- Other estimators also use log loss by default for similar purposes (early stopping)
  - `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` defaults to `scoring=loss` which uses log loss.
  - `GradientBoostingClassifier` uses training loss function which defaults to log loss.

@scikit-learn/core-devs @scikit-learn/communication-team @scikit-learn/documentation-team

title: `pairwise_distances` throws warnings with array API classes
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

According to the docs:
https://scikit-learn.org/dev/modules/array_api.html

`pairwise_distances` should have support for array API for metrics like euclidean.

But it appears to still rely on functions with numpy-specific code:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/ad136afbe4d316f219d8d770d15a76a1b5e9cd05/sklearn/utils/extmath.py#L219

import os

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)

Xa = array_api_strict.from_dlpack(X)

title: FIX _set_order for 1D SciPy sparse arrays (*_array) when converting to CSC/CSR
body:
### Describe the bug

On recent SciPy versions (e.g. SciPy 1.16.3 used in CI), sparse **array** containers (`coo_array`, `csr_array`, etc.) can be **1-D** (shape `(n_samples,)`). However, scikit-learn, `_set_order` assumes any sparse `y` can be converted to CSC/CSR and calls `y.asformat("csc")` when `order="F"`, but SciPy raises:

`ValueError: Cannot convert a 1d sparse array to csc format`

So far this issue did not surface because the original test `test_set_order_sparse` added in #15436 (commit 21686b7) contained a typo. It used `y = X.asformat(sparse_format)` instead of `y = y.asformat(sparse_format)`. When fixing/generalizing that test as part of #32991, the test started exercising `_set_order` with a real sparse `y`, which revealed the failure on newer SciPy sparse arrays.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce
1. for `_set_order`
```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import sparse
from sklearn.linear_model._coordinate_descent import _set_order

X = sparse.coo_array(np.array([[0], [0], [0]])).asformat("csr")
y = sparse.coo_array(np.array([0, 0, 0])).asformat("csr")
_set_order(X, y, order="F")
```

2. for `test_set_order_sparse` ( if we convert `y = X.asformat(sparse_format)` to `y = y.asformat(sparse_format)` ) 
```python
from sklearn.utils.fixes import COO_CONTAINERS, CSC_CONTAINERS, CSR_CONTAINERS
X = COO_CONTAINERS[1](np.array([[0], [0], [0]]))
y = COO_CONTAINERS[1](np.array([0, 0, 0]))

```

title: Duplicate check_array parameter usage in pairwise.py for X and Y inputs
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py` (lines ~167–202), `check_array` is called with identical parameters for both `X` and `Y` when they are different objects.

Current behavior:
- If `Y is X` or `Y is None`, `check_array` is called once.
- Otherwise, `check_array` is called separately for both `X` and `Y` using the same arguments.

This leads to duplicated parameter passing and slightly reduced code maintainability. Additionally, `_find_floating_dtype_allow_sparse` already processes both inputs, making this repetition unnecessary from a structural perspective.

Impact: No functional issue, but introduces redundancy and reduces code clarity.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

X = np.random.rand(100, 10)
Y = np.random.rand(100, 10)

cosine_similarity(X, Y)

# Internally, check_array is called twice with identical parameters
```

### Expected Results

Common parameters for `check_array` should be consolidated to avoid duplication and improve readability.

### Actual Results

`check_array` is invoked separately for `X` and `Y` with identical parameters, leading to duplicated code paths.

### Versions

```shell
import sklearn
sklearn.show_versions()
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No, I would be interested in working on a PR.

My approach:
- Extract common `check_array` parameters into a shared configuration.
- Apply the same configuration to both `X` and `Y` without duplicating argument definitions.
- Ensure behavior remains unchanged by running existing tests.

Additionally, I would review nearby code for similar duplication patterns and refactor them where applicable to improve overall consistency.

title: Add Net Benefit for classifications metrics
body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Net benefit is defined as a decision-analytic measure that quantifies the clinical value of a prediction model, test, or marker by putting its benefits and harms on the same scale. This is done by specifying an exchange rate—a clinical judgment about how much a harm (e.g., an unnecessary biopsy) can be tolerated in order to gain a benefit (e.g., detecting a cancer). The net benefit calculation then subtracts weighted harms from benefits to determine whether using the model or test would do more good than harm in practice, unlike traditional statistics such as sensitivity or AUC that do not directly reflect clinical value.

https://www.bmj.com/content/352/bmj.i6

body: ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact The chance_level line drawn by `PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions` when `plot_chance_level=True` is not correct when `y_true` is an instance of `pytorch.Tensor`. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python # pytorch==2.8.0 from sklearn.metrics import PrecisionRecallDisplay import torch torch.manual_seed(42) y_true = torch.cat([torch.ones(40), torch.zeros(60)]) # Chance level equal 0.4 y_score = torch.rand_like(y_true) PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions(y_true, y_score, plot_chance_level=True) # Wrong PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions(y_true.numpy(), y_score, plot_chance_level=True) # Correct ``` ### Expected Results Correct chance classifier line at y 0.4 with y_true as a numpy array. ### Actual Results Wrong chance classifier line at y 0.0 with y_true as a pytorch tensor. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.13.5 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Jun 12 2025, 16:37:03) [MSC v.1929 64 bit (AMD64)] executable: C:\Users\lucas\miniconda\envs\pytorch28\python.exe machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.7.1 pip: 25.1 setuptools: 78.1.1 numpy: 2.1.2 libiomp filepath: C:\Users\lucas\miniconda\envs\pytorch28\Lib\site-packages\torch\lib\libiomp5md.dll version: None user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 1 prefix: libiomp filepath: C:\Users\lucas\miniconda\envs\pytorch28\Lib\site-packages\torch\lib\libiompstubs5md.dll version: None user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 12 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: C:\Users\lucas\miniconda\envs\pytorch28\Lib\site-packages\numpy.libs\libscipy_openblas64_-c16e4918366c6bc1f1cd71e28ca36fc0.dll version: 0.3.27 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 12 prefix: vcomp filepath: C:\Users\lucas\miniconda\envs\pytorch28\Lib\site-packages\sklearn\.libs\vcomp140.dll version: None user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 12 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: C:\Users\lucas\miniconda\envs\pytorch28\Lib\site-packages\scipy.libs\libscipy_openblas-6b2103f2ae4d8547998b5d188e9801fb.dll version: 0.3.28 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Working on this, the root cause is due to these reasons: - pytorch (and potentially other array libraries) defines scalars in such a way that their hash is different from their value and same values may have different hashes; - `PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions` relies on `Counter` class to compare `y_true` entries with `pos_label` values in order to generate `prevalence_pos_label` (chance level). https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/646da0f072a8afef6a980aa427a710311e67eb9d/sklearn/metrics/_plot/precision_recall_curve.py#L563-L565 - `Counter` is not able to group objects with same values since they have different hash values. Comparing the values from `y_true` directly to `pos_label` to calculate `prevalence_pos_label` should be enough to fix this.

comments.author: lucolivi
comments.body:
As per line [R481](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/62389681eafb4609b70426c81b0223e8bcea9d2a#diff-5f3c744abb22f57ee2bd1ee7515d6e9dd2462de9ddc60e487da9ce666b6d746dR481), its the first implementation from 3 years ago. Most likely the author used `Counter` for convenience only.

I think `prevalence_pos_label = (y_true == pos_label).sum() / len(y_true)` will break in case `y_true` and `pos_label` are neither complied with ArrayAPI, like native list and integers.

Despite the problem simplicity, I like the `check_array` solution to keep things more high level.

About testings, since `.from_predictions` returns the display object containing `prevalence_pos_label` property, we could check if its value is correct.

In a broader scenario, should this pytorch behavior be a big concern? Perhaps adding some monkey-patched warnings in the test suite in case array libraries are used to index dict like objects?

comments.author: lesteve
comments.body:
Good point that `y_true` is array-like so it can be a list. In this case using something like `y_true = check_array(y_true, ensure_2d=False)` at the top of the function seems to make sense.

I would also use something like `prevalence_pos_label = (y_true == pos_label).sum() / len(y_true)` for simplicity rather than the current `Counter` code.

Inspecting the label for the AP value seems OK (even if a bit brittle) as a test if you can make it work.

The topic here is that a PyTorch CPU tensor is array-like and that `.from_predictions` documents `y_true` as array-like. In other words, providing a PyTorch CPU tensor is supposed to work for array-like inputs because the PyTorch CPU tensor will be converted to a numpy array by scikit-learn code (`check_array` that does something like `np.asarray` at one point).

Array API support is something slightly different, it's the ability (ongoing experimental effort, see [doc](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/array_api.html)) to keep the PyTorch [^1] tensor (CPU or GPU) and do the computation with PyTorch throughout the scikit-learn code.

[^1]: also other libraries like CuPy and others that conform to the Array API spec

title: MAINT: Improve array API consistency in _validate_shuffle_split
body:
### Current Problem

The helper function `_validate_shuffle_split` (used by `train_test_split`, `ShuffleSplit`, `StratifiedShuffleSplit`, etc.) still uses NumPy-specific patterns (`np.asarray`, `.dtype.kind`, etc.).

Other parts of the same file (`StratifiedKFold`, `StratifiedShuffleSplit`, etc.) have already been updated to support the Array API using `get_namespace` and `move_to`.

This creates inconsistency inside `_split.py`.

### Why it matters
scikit-learn is actively improving Array API support across the library. Small inconsistencies make future maintenance harder and limit compatibility with non-NumPy arrays (such as CuPy).

### Proposed Improvement

Make `_validate_shuffle_split` more consistent with the rest of the module by:
- Using `get_namespace` where appropriate
- Handling array API inputs gracefully while keeping the current NumPy behavior unchanged

**Location**:  
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` → `_validate_shuffle_split` function

I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this small maintenance task once the issue is triaged.

title: Add a warning whenever `metrics.confusion_matrix` is called with non-numeric values but no labels provided
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Whenever an array-like of string types for a multi-class classification problem is passed into the `confusion_matrix` function without an argument passed for labels, the confusion matrix is returned with the classes in alphabetical order.
While this is expected behaviour and the natural way to sort anything string-like, the outputted confusion matrix may have an output order that is different from the user's expectations, especially if the classes are ordinal. Since the output of the `confusion_matrix` function is an array, without any explicit labels, this means it will need to be manually re-aligned with the labels. 
There is currently no warning for this, possibly leading to misunderstood confusions matrices by users.

### Describe your proposed solution

Near the start of the `confusion_matrix` function, check if the type of the arrays are string-like (or another type without an inherent order) and if `labels` is `None`, i.e. the default value. If this condition is True, raise a warning for the user that their confusion matrix will be returned in alphabetical order.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

There is a valid alternative view that the user should be aware their inputs have no natural order, unless provided, and so should take responsibility for the validity of their inputs. However, this proposed warning would not affect a small number of use cases and would induce a very small computational overhead

### Additional context

_No response_
author: conor-hamill

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
Thanks for your suggestion, @conor-hamill.

I can see how that could lead people to mis-interprete their `confusion_matrix`, but nonetheless I would tend to not add a new `Warning` here.

The reason is that in scikit-learn we try to only add warnings if a user likely needs to take action on it (such like in a deprecation) and rely on documentation otherwise. Warnings are barely read and can feel annoying or overwhelming to users, especially if we add to many. 

In this case, we have documented the behaviour:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b9a147f2d9f3d80d142ed4b02f8d401c140272bf/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py#L454-L455

And a user who is aware of the string label sorting would not need to take any action, so we don't want to force them to pass labels only to suppress a warning.

I will therefore close this issue. Happy to reopen it if other maintainers feel differently about this.

---
Not sure, but is a warning like that maybe an interesting feature for [skore](https://github.com/probabl-ai/skore), @GaetandeCast?

title: Hopefully Helpful (AI) Contributing Policy Proposal
body:
I saw a [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ssTUhnShKGM) about the Open Source Community problems related to AI Contributing and I saw your [Issue](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/31679) related to that. 

In another video, there was also mention of a proposed solution that GitHub could even have developed.
2 months later, GitHub has still not developed it, and there was a video in recent days suggesting that it might actually be better that GitHub did not develop it.
https://github.com/marketplace/actions/ai-pull-request-equalizer#credits

So I made a very simple GitHub Action:

- If someone has a defined — configurable — permission on GitHub (for example admin/pull), then they can open a PR.
- If someone has at least 1 open Issue assigned to them, they can open a PR.
- If they do not meet either of the above conditions, then they receive a message to channel their energy to a place where there is a shortage of them.

This is a bit different from your current 'You can open PRs to not Needs Triage Issues after commenting under them'.

If you find it useful, then in your current flow I could imagine it as follows:
- Either you allow an always open issue for an external contributor (for example a 'I am not an AI introduction: I would like to contribute to scikit-learn' issue)
- Or you explicitly assign the issue to the person who indicated in a comment that they are working on it. (A human contributor takes far more time than this to complete it, and the AI contributor does not have a sense of time, it does not wait)

Why I think my solution is better than the competing ones:
Simple installation (you only need to copy+paste one file), transparent rules and It redirects AI contributors instead of blocking them — less likely to trigger a strong reaction.

If I have piqued your interest, you can find it here:
https://github.com/marketplace/actions/ai-pull-request-equalizer

title: Document tie-breaking behavior for max_categories in OneHotEncoder/OrdinalEncoder infrequent category grouping
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation



When `max_categories` forces additional categories into the infrequent group beyond what `min_frequency` alone would select, and multiple categories are tied in count at the cutoff boundary, the docs for `max_categories` don't specify which tied category is kept as frequent vs. grouped as infrequent.

Looking at `_identify_infrequent()` in `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`, the tie-break is implicit rather than documented:

```python
# stable sort to preserve original count order
smallest_levels = np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")[:-frequent_category_count]
infrequent_mask[smallest_levels] = True
```

Counts are sorted using `np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")` — a stable sort — so ties are resolved by the order categories appear in `categories_[i]`, which for `categories='auto'` is lexicographic/numeric sort order. This behavior is not mentioned in the `max_categories` docstring or the User Guide section on infrequent categories (`encoder_infrequent_categories`).

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a sentence to the `max_categories` parameter docs (in both `OneHotEncoder` and `OrdinalEncoder`) and to the User Guide section on infrequent categories, stating that ties in category count are broken using the sort order of the categories (via a stable sort). This is also relevant to the discussion in #32161.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

X = np.array([["a"] * 2 + ["b"] * 2 + ["c"] * 5], dtype=object).T
enc = OneHotEncoder(max_categories=2, sparse_output=False).fit(X)
print(enc.infrequent_categories_)
# 'a' and 'b' tie at count=2 -- which one is grouped as infrequent
# is not documented, though it is deterministic.
```

### Additional context

Related: #32161 discusses tie-breaking by lexicographical order for encoder category ordering more broadly.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

KMeans does not produce expected centers update after 1 iteration.

Context: I was trying to use sklearn as a reference to debug a custom kmeans implementation and found this unexpected behavior.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

With `sample_weights = np.ones(...)`, I'd expect `weight_in_clusters[i] == np.sum(labels == i)`, but it's not the case.

Run with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`:

title: BUG _parallel_pairwise does not slice Y_norm_squared alongside Y when n_jobs > 1
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`_parallel_pairwise` chunks `Y` into slices for parallel execution but passes `**kwds` (including `Y_norm_squared`) unchanged. When `euclidean_distances` is called with `Y_norm_squared` and `n_jobs > 1`, this causes a `ValueError` due to shape mismatch between the sliced `Y` and the full `Y_norm_squared`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import _parallel_pairwise, euclidean_distances
import numpy as np

X = np.random.RandomState(42).rand(13, 4)
Y_norm_squared = np.sum(X ** 2, axis=1)

# n_jobs=1: no chunking, Y_norm_squared matches Y — works fine
result = _parallel_pairwise(X, X, euclidean_distances, n_jobs=1, Y_norm_squared=Y_norm_squared)
print("n_jobs=1: OK", result.shape)

# n_jobs=2: Y chunked but Y_norm_squared stays full — crashes
_parallel_pairwise(X, X, euclidean_distances, n_jobs=2, Y_norm_squared=Y_norm_squared)
```

### Expected Results

No error is thrown. The `n_jobs=2` call returns the same distance matrix as `n_jobs=1`.

### Actual Results

```python-traceback
ValueError: Incompatible dimensions for Y of shape (6, 4) and Y_norm_squared of shape (13,).
```

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.12.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Feb  6 2025, 12:55:12) [Clang 14.0.6 ]
   machine: macOS-26.4.1-arm64-arm-64bit

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.8.0
          pip: 25.0
   setuptools: 82.0.1
        numpy: 2.4.4
        scipy: 1.17.1
       Cython: 3.2.4
       pandas: 2.3.3
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

Also confirmed on `main` (the code at `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py` line 1986 still passes `**kwds` unsliced).

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes — I have a fix ready in #33876. The fix slices `Y_norm_squared` alongside `Y` in the `Parallel` call inside `_parallel_pairwise()`.

title: CI Add aggregating job in GHA to summarize statuses of all unit test jobs and be used a required check
body: Follow-up on https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/32434, the idea would be to have a single ggregating job (green if all unit test jobs are green, red if one of the unit test is red) to use it as required checks. Azure had a built-in aggregated job which we were using for our required check and right now our GHA required checks are based on a number of exact job names which is a bit brittle. From a quick look some time ago https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31832#issuecomment-3116678817: - [github.com/orgs/community/discussions/4324#discussioncomment-13335158](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/4324#discussioncomment-13335158) - third-party GitHub action [re-actors/alls-green](https://github.com/re-actors/alls-green?rgh-link-date=2025-07-25T07%3A08%3A55Z) that seems to handle this use case I am wondering whether if this is doable/easy to take into account the status "optional" jobs, for example free-threaded or scipy-dev in a PR. ---------------- More details, GitHub required checks are managed centrally via the web UI on a job level and are based on exact job names. Setting is [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/settings/branch_protection_rules/23621449) That means that it you change a job name in `main` and then update the required checks, all the PRs will have a pending job that never complete and the PR can not be merged. The work-around is to merge `main` into your PR branch. Having a single aggregating job used a I think @FrancoisPgm had an initial look at one point, feel free to add more relevant context if you have some.

title: learning_curve  with exploit_incremental_learning=True fails to compute training scores when  sample_weight  is provided
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using learning_curve with exploit_incremental_learning=True and passing sample_weight
 (or other parameters) to the scorer, the training scores for all training sizes except the final one are returned as NaN.

This happens because _incremental_fit_estimator pre-computes the training scores' parameters once for the full training set, but then attempts to use them for subsets of the training data. This causes a ValueError (consistent length mismatch) inside the scorer, which is silently caught and replaced with NaN.

This affects any user trying to evaluate learning curves incrementally while using weighted metrics or metadata-aware scorers.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```py
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.metrics import make_scorer, accuracy_score
import sklearn

# Enable metadata routing to pass sample_weight to scorer
sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=5, random_state=42)
weights = np.ones(100)
scorer = make_scorer(accuracy_score).set_score_request(sample_weight=True)

train_sizes, train_scores, _ = learning_curve(
    SGDClassifier(), X, y, 
    train_sizes=[0.3, 0.6, 0.9],
    cv=3,
    exploit_incremental_learning=True,
    scoring=scorer,
    params={'sample_weight': weights}
)

print("Training scores (expecting no NaNs):")
print(train_scores)
```

### Expected Results

The training scores should be successfully computed for all training sizes. Example: [[0.96 0.96 0.96], [0.94 0.94 0.94], [0.92 0.92 0.92]] (no NaN values).

### Actual Results

```
[[ nan  nan  nan]
 [ nan  nan  nan]
 [0.93 0.95 0.92]]
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.14.2
    machine: Windows-10
Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.8.0.dev0
        numpy: 2.4.1
        scipy: 1.17.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in fixing this.
author: atheendre130505

title: Performance issue with HTML representations of estimators with 'many' features with sklearn 1.9.0
body: Nilearn uses the HTML representation of sklearn for its estimators. Running the following notebook for fitting a simple masker gives a VERY sluggish browsing experience. ```bash pip install marimo scikit-learn==1.9.0 nilearn==0.13.1 ``` ```python import marimo __generated_with = "0.23.9" app = marimo.App(width="full") @app.cell def _(): from nilearn.datasets import load_mni152_gm_template from nilearn.maskers import NiftiMasker gm_template = load_mni152_gm_template() masker = NiftiMasker( mask_img=gm_template, standardize="zscore_sample", memory="nilearn_cache", memory_level=1, target_affine=gm_template.affine, target_shape=gm_template.shape, ) masker return (masker,) @app.cell def _(masker): from nilearn.datasets import load_sample_motor_activation_image data = load_sample_motor_activation_image() masker.fit(data) masker return @app.cell def _(masker): report = masker.generate_report() report return if __name__ == "__main__": app.run() ``` I believe that this is due to the fact that sklearn HTML representation now give a list of the features which in our case can be quite large. This also affects the browsing experience of our own home made HTML reports. Running the same notebook with sklearn 1.8.0 gives a different and more fluid experience. This is not a bug but definitely affects user experience. I wonder if anyone else has run into similar issues and what could possibly done to change this.

Therefore, I see at least two possible ways to move the discussion forward: 1. If I were familiar with `nilearn`’s codebase, I would check whether [NiftiMasker](https://nilearn.github.io/dev/modules/generated/nilearn.maskers.NiftiMasker.html) depends on [ColumnTransformer](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.compose.ColumnTransformer.html#sklearn.compose.ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out) in any way. 1. jeremiedbb
comments.body:
Thanks for the report @Remi-Gau. The html repr relies inspects the fitted attributes through the results of ``__dir__``. It looks like nilearn choses to raise a ValueError when trying to access these attributes and not an AttributeError (which __dir__ would naturally ignore).

I would argue that raising a ValueError to signal that an attribute is not available is fragile. For instance ``hasattr`` returns True. A simple and robust solution would be to raise an ``AttributeError``.

Another solution could be to reimplement ``_get_fitted_attrs_html`` to fit nilearn's declaration of unavailable attrs. I don't think that sklearn should to the filtering: for many downstream packages it would just risk to hide bugs.

title: [BUG] BayesianRidge.predict with return_std=True fails to center test features, leading to incorrect predictive variance
body: ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In `BayesianRidge`, the predictive variance calculation in the `predict` method is mathematically inconsistent with the training process when `fit_intercept=True` (the default). During `fit()`, the model centers the features (`X - X_offset_`), but during `predict()`, the variance is calculated using the **raw** test features `X_test` instead of centering them by the training mean `X_offset_`. As a result, the model reports its lowest uncertainty at the coordinate origin rather than at the center of the training data. For datasets far from the origin, this leads to significantly wrong uncertainty estimation, violating the principle that a Bayesian model should be most certain in the region where it has observed the most data. #### Mathematical formulation The original problem is $y = w^T x + b + \epsilon$. Instead, scikit-learn solves a centered version $y = w^T \tilde{x} + b' + \epsilon$, where $\tilde{x} = x - E[x]$, in order to find $w$ and $b'$, and finally $b$ is computed as $b = b' - w^T E[x]$. First, $b'$ is estimated using a frequentist approach (OLS/MLE) to be $b' = E[y]$, since $E[\tilde{x}] = 0$. This allows the problem to be reduced to $\tilde{y} = y - b' = w^T \tilde{x} + \epsilon$, on which a Bayesian approach is used to find $w$ (the posterior mean). After $w$ is found, the predictive distribution of $\tilde{y}$ on a new test point $\tilde{x}$ is then given by $$\tilde{\mu} = w^T \tilde{x}$$ $$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + \tilde{x}^T \Sigma_w \tilde{x}$$ But since $y = \tilde{y} + b'$, the predictive distribution of $y$ has the mean shifted to $$\mu = w^T \tilde{x} + b'$$ while the variance stays the same. However, our test point is actually $x$, so this all becomes $$\mu = w^T (x - \mu_x) + b' = w^T x + b$$ $$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + (x - \mu_x)^T \Sigma_w (x - \mu_x)$$ where $\mu_x = E[x]$ (estimated using the training data). Note that `predict` returns `y_mean` and `y_std`, where `y_mean` is exactly $\mu$, but `y_std` is not $\sigma$; instead it is $$\alpha^{-1} + x^T \Sigma_w x$$ What is missing is to subtract $\mu_x$ from $x$ before the variance computation. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import BayesianRidge n = 4 x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n) y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n) model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101) y_mean, y_std = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True) print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}") print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}") plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.') plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-') plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue') plt.title('Actual Results') plt.show() x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n) x_train -= x_train.mean() y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n) model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101) y_mean, y_std = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True) print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}") print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}") plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.') plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-') plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue') plt.title('Correct when data is already centered') plt.show() x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n) y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n) model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101) y_mean = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1)) _, y_std = model.predict((x - model.X_offset_).reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True) print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}") print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}") plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.') plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-') plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue') plt.title('Expected Results') plt.show() ``` ### Expected Results Lowest variance close to the training data. ### Actual Results Lowest variance close to the origin. Note that this is fine if the data is already centered; this is the problem scikit-learn is actually solving. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.14.2 (main, Jan 27 2026, 23:59:57) [Clang 21.1.4 ] executable: /home/danilo/sciml/.venv/bin/python machine: Linux-6.17.0-20-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.42 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.8.0 pip: None setuptools: 81.0.0 numpy: 2.4.2 scipy: 1.17.0 Cython: None pandas: 3.0.0 matplotlib: 3.10.8 joblib: 1.5.3 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 24 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/danilo/sciml/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-096271d3.so version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: SkylakeX user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 24 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/danilo/sciml/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-6cdc3b4a.so version: 0.3.30 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: SkylakeX user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 24 prefix: libgomp filepath: /home/danilo/sciml/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scikit_learn.libs/libgomp-e985bcbb.so.1.0.0 version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug The bug is very easy to fix: just add a single line subtracting the mean before the variance calculation. ```python def predict(self, X, return_std=False): y_mean = self._decision_function(X) if not return_std: return y_mean else: X = X - self.X_offset_ # <-- just add this line sigmas_squared_data = (np.dot(X, self.sigma_) * X).sum(axis=1) y_std = np.sqrt(sigmas_squared_data + (1.0 / self.alpha_)) return y_mean, y_std ```

title: ENH: Add confusion_matrix_diff to compare multiple models against a baseline
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When comparing classification models, users frequently need to understand how one model differs from another on a per-class basis. The current workflow requires manually computing separate confusion matrices and subtracting them:

```
cm1 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_baseline)
cm2 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_model2)
diff = cm2 - cm1
```

This pattern has no built-in support in sklearn and becomes error-prone when normalization is involved - normalizing before vs after subtraction gives different results and users may not be aware of this distinction.

There is also no standard scalable way to compare multiple models against a single baseline in one call.

### Describe your proposed solution

Add confusion_matrix_diff to sklearn.metrics with the following signature:

```
def confusion_matrix_diff(
    y_true_or_cm_baseline,
    *args,
    precomputed=False,
    labels=None,
    sample_weight=None,
    normalize=None
)
```

**Label mode (precomputed=False):**

```
# Two models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2)

# Three models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, y_pred3)

# With normalization
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, normalize='true')
```

**Precomputed mode (precomputed=True):**

`result = confusion_matrix_diff(cm_baseline, cm2, cm3, precomputed=True)`

Returns a 3D array of shape (n_comparisons, n_classes, n_classes) where:
- Positive values = comparison model better than baseline
- Negative values = baseline better than comparison model

The normalize parameter mirrors confusion_matrix exactly - normalization is applied to each matrix individually before subtraction, giving meaningful per-class rate differences rather than raw count differences.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Users can subtract confusion matrices manually, but this does not handle:
- Consistent normalization across matrices before subtraction
- Multi-model comparison in a single call
- Input validation for mismatched label sets or matrix shapes

A utility function makes this discoverable, correct by default, and consistent with the existing confusion_matrix API.

### Additional context

- No changes to existing functions — additions only
- Placement: sklearn/metrics/_classification.py alongside confusion_matrix
- Exported from sklearn.metrics
- Full numpydoc docstring and tests included in the PR

Happy to adjust the API design based on maintainer feedback before writing any code.

title: `KNeighborsClassifier` fails on non-numeric labels with `ValueError` on certain parameters combination
body:
### Describe the bug

When used with `algorithm="brute"` (or `algorithm="auto"` and the heuristic suggests brute force) and `p = 1`, `KNeighborsClassifier.predict` crashes when y labels are non-integers.

Note that this only crashes for this specific param combination, and `p=2`, for example, works fine with non-integer labels.

This happens because `self.classes_` is passed to `unique_Y_labels` here:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/66200f149ba6c64a3a93dd73e37bdeea87bb5db8/sklearn/neighbors/_classification.py#L358

And the [docs](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/66200f149ba6c64a3a93dd73e37bdeea87bb5db8/sklearn/metrics/_pairwise_distances_reduction/_dispatcher.py#L514-L516) for `ArgKminClassMode.compute` say:

```
        unique_Y_labels : ndarray
            An array containing all unique indices contained in the
            corresponding `Y_labels` array.
```

while `self.classes_` contains actual values, not indices.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import random

import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# generate random data
rng = np.random.default_rng()
x = rng.normal(size=(5, 3))
y = random.choices(['foo', 'bar'], k=5)

kn = KNeighborsClassifier(algorithm='brute', p=1)
kn = kn.fit(x, y)
kn.predict(rng.normal(size=(2, 3)))
```

### Expected Results

No error.

### Actual Results

```python-traceback

  File "/home/stas/Documents/Work/polymerize/ml_dev/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/sklearn/neighbors/_classification.py", line 266, in predict
    probabilities = self.predict_proba(X)
                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    probabilities = ArgKminClassMode.compute(

    unique_Y_labels=np.array(unique_Y_labels, dtype=np.intp),
                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: np.str_('bar')
```

Then it can be removed completely, only passing the total count of classes instead.

comments.body:
As discussed, the crash happens because unique_Y_labels receives raw string labels from self.classes_, but the underlying ArgKminClassMode implementation expects integer types (even if it only uses the shape).

I've implemented a fix using np.arange(len(self.classes_), dtype=np.intp) to pass the correct indices, which solves the crash without modifying the Cython extensions.

I'm working on the PR and will submit it shortly.

comments.body: Apologies, I am a new contributor and I didn't notice the rule about waiting for the 'Needs Triage' label to be removed. I just wanted to help fix the crash. Please let me know if I need to adjust anything.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
I agree this is a bug. The docstring of the `ArgKminClassMode.compute` method states that  `Y_labels` is "An array containing the index of the class membership of the associated samples in `Y`. This is used in labeling `X`."

So both `Y_labels` and `unique_Y_labels` are expected to be encoded as integers prior to passing them to `ArgKminClassMode.compute`.

EDIT: I confirm that `self._y` is always manually integer encoded at fit time in the base class: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b76422979fc4d215d8063dc27e4b8acdcd33c60d/sklearn/neighbors/_base.py#L506-L509. So passing raw labels in the `unique_Y_labels` values is inconsistent.

comments.author: sterliakov
comments.body: Yes, that matches my observations. Looking at `ArgKminClassMode` implementation, it seems like this array can be avoided altogether, it only looks at its `.shape[0]` - passing just a number of classes could be more efficient?

comments.author: Crescens-beep
comments.body:
Hi! I'm interested in working on this issue as part of my preparation for GSoC. 

I've reproduced the bug and understand the problem - `self.classes_` contains actual label values but `ArgKminClassMode.compute` expects label indices. The fix would likely involve passing `np.arange(len(self.classes_))` or using `np.searchsorted` to convert labels to indices before passing to the function.

Note that changing backend to `loky` fixes the behavior.

this probably comes from a bad deserialization of the params as a dict instead of a `Bunch` but it is unclear why it only happens for `dask`.

comments.author: adrinjalali
comments.body:
This is the root of the cause, which is not idea, since it's ignoring the child classes of `dict`:

```py
  >>> from distributed.protocol import dumps, loads
  >>> from sklearn.utils import Bunch
  >>> type(loads(dumps(Bunch(transform={'a':1}))))
  <class 'dict'>
```

and `dask` backend uses this. We can fix it in sklearn by not using the bunch syntax, but I think the issue needs to be fixed on the dask backend side. WDYT?

title: Add 'quantile' strategy to `calibration_curve`
body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Choose between different binning strategies ("uniform" fixed width bins, "quantile" equal mass bins) to estimate the calibration curve.

### Describe your proposed solution

Adding in `calibration_curve` a new `strategy = "uniform"` or `strategy = "quantile"` option to switch between the two binning strategies. We can for now just add the option and change the default in a follow up PR.

We can also add (in the same or follow up PR) the `strategy="isotonic"`  option to implement the CORP approach as advocated in #23132.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

There are multiple issues / PRs on implementing calibration metrics (for example the expected calibration error, the Brier score decomposition) and improving reliability diagrams:  
#18268, #11096,  #22233, #21774, #23767,  #23132

There are two main ways to estimate the calibration curve (and metrics):
1. using binning, either "uniform" (fixed-width bins) or "quantile" (equal mass bins)
2. using isotonic regression, this is the [CORP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) approach, see #23132

For the binning case, the quality of the estimate in the binning depends crucially on 
1a. the number of bins, it seems that `n_bins=n**(1/3)` is best, this is tackled by #33856
1b. the binning strategy, it seems that "quantile" is better, see [Roelofs et al](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08668) or [Nixon et al](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.01685) 

Reading through the literature, I feel that the "best estimator for the calibration curve/metrics" is not yet settled.   Based on the experiments reported in the [CORP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) paper, the isotonic regression seems the most accurate. However there are ways to debias the binned estimates for the Brier score decomposition that we could investigate, see [Ferro and Fricker, 2012](https://empslocal.ex.ac.uk/people/staff/ferro/Publications/ferro-fricker2012copyright.pdf).

Also, we might want the different options with each its own benefits: fixed-width bins to visually compare different curves or put them in a dataframe, equal mass bins to get a more reliable curve with a manageable length (`n_bins = n**(1/3)`), isotonic regression for its accuracy but at the expense of  a crowded curve (length `n`).

Overall, having the different options seems to me the best way for further implementations of the calibration metrics or curve, without having to commit to one option over another.

cc @ogrisel @lorentzenchr
author: antoinebaker

comments.body: Ah my bad the option already exist. Closing in favor of issue #23132 for adding the isotonic regression approach, this is tackled by the PR #23824.
