title: OneHotEncoder unknown-category warning is incorrect for columns without an infrequent category
body:
### Introduce yourself

I'm learning ML engineering and use scikit-learn for a delay-prediction model on
US flight data. This is the first issue I've opened. I encountered this while working out how to encode categorical columns that may contain previously unseen values during prediction.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Carrier and destination can't be enumerated ahead of time, so both go to one
encoder with `drop="first"`, `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"` and
`min_frequency=4`. On my first CV fold, 41,901 rows, it fits to:

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['HDN'], dtype=object)]
```

Destination gets an infrequent bucket. Carrier gets `None` because its rarest value has 148 rows in that fold and 744 across the training pool, so it is not below `min_frequency=4`. Transforming a row with an unknown carrier and an unknown destination produces this warning:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown
categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

The warning claims that the unknown categories in both columns will go to the infrequent category, but this is not true for the carrier feature because no `infrequent_sklearn` column exists for it, and the transformed row is zero across the entire carrier block.

This matters because `drop="first"` drops the encoded feature for the first carrier category (`AA` in this fold), making all zeros its carrier encoding. An unknown airline and a real flight belonging to `AA` therefore produce an identical carrier encoding, so the model treats them the same with respect to the carrier feature.

I caught this by inspecting `infrequent_categories_`, transforming a row containing an unknown carrier and destination, and comparing the resulting vector with `get_feature_names_out()`. The carrier block was entirely zero, even though the warning said that the unknown carrier would be encoded as the infrequent category. The warning should have identified that the unknown carrier was encoded as all zeros, while the unknown destination was routed to its infrequent bucket.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import warnings

from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

# Column 0: "a" and "b" both appear twice, so it has no infrequent category.
# Column 1: "y" appears once, so it does have an infrequent category.
X = [["a", "x"], ["a", "x"], ["b", "x"], ["b", "y"]]

encoder = OneHotEncoder(
    drop="first",
    sparse_output=False,
    handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
    min_frequency=2,
).fit(X)

print("infrequent_categories_:", encoder.infrequent_categories_)
print("feature names:         ", encoder.get_feature_names_out())

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    X_trans = encoder.transform([["c", "z"]])

print("transform([['c', 'z']]):", X_trans)
print("warning:", caught[0].message)
```

Both columns receive an unknown category, but only column 1 has an infrequent
category that can absorb it.


### Expected Results

The warning should describe what actually happens to each column. Column 1 has
an infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded there. Column 0 has
no infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded as all zeros, which is the same encoding `drop="first"` assigns to the dropped category.

Something along the lines of:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. The unknown
categories in columns [1] will be encoded as the infrequent category. Those in
columns [0] will be encoded as all zeros, because these columns have no
infrequent category.
```

This is also what the `handle_unknown` docstring already documents:

> If the `'infrequent'` category does not exist, then `transform` and
> `inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
> `handle_unknown='ignore'`.


### Actual Results

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['y'], dtype=object)]
feature names:          ['x0_b' 'x1_infrequent_sklearn']
transform([['c', 'z']]): [[0. 1.]]
warning: Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

No exception is raised. The problem is that the warning talks about both columns and
makes a single claim about them, which is false for column 0: its
`infrequent_categories_` entry is `None`, no `x0_infrequent_sklearn` column
exists in `get_feature_names_out()`, and the transformed row is `0` across the
whole column-0 block.

Also reproduced on main (1.10.dev0) at a456b324bc, with identical output.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 21 2025, 19:11:29) [Clang 20.1.8 ]
   machine: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
          pip: 25.2
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.2
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: 3.0.5
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.25.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in opening a PR if this is triaged as a bug.

The warning message is selected once from `handle_unknown`, but the actual outcome is determined separately for each column in `_map_infrequent_categories` (`sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`). I would update the warning to distinguish columns that have an infrequent category from those that fall back to all zeros, update the affected warning assertions, and add a regression test for the mixed case above.
author: karansgotit

comments.author: sundeep8967
comments.body:
Hi maintainers,

I have prepared a fix for this issue in `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`.

### Approach:
When `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`, `columns_with_unknown` is partitioned into:
1. `infrequent_cols`: Columns that have an infrequent category (`self._infrequent_indices[i] is not None`).
2. `zeros_cols`: Columns that do not have an infrequent category (`self._infrequent_indices[i] is None`), which fall back to all zeros.

The warning message is then tailored to describe:
- If all columns have an infrequent category: *"These unknown categories will be encoded as the infrequent category."*
- If all columns lack an infrequent category: *"These unknown categories will be encoded as all zeros, because these columns have no infrequent category."*
- If mixed: *"The unknown categories in columns [...] will be encoded as the infrequent category. Those in columns [...] will be encoded as all zeros, because these columns have no infrequent category."*

We also added regression test `test_ohe_unknown_category_warning_mixed_infrequent` in `sklearn/preprocessing/tests/test_encoders.py`.

Could maintainers please review if this approach aligns with expectations so `Needs Triage` can be resolved?

comments.author: ammar-iitm
comments.body:
Hi @karansgotit, thanks for the clear write-up and repro.

I dug into this and confirmed the root cause: in `_BaseEncoder._transform`, the `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"` branch builds a single `columns_with_unknown` list and always emits the "will be encoded as the infrequent category" message for every column in it — but a column only actually falls back to the infrequent category if `self._infrequent_indices[i] is not None` for that column (see `_map_infrequent_categories`). A column with no infrequent category at all (e.g. no category was ever below `min_frequency`, or infrequent grouping isn't enabled) is instead encoded as all zeros, so the warning is wrong for that column.

I put together a fix that partitions `columns_with_unknown` into "has an infrequent category" vs. "doesn't", and emits a separate, accurate warning for each group:

```python
>>> import warnings
>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
>>> X = [["a", "x"], ["a", "x"], ["b", "x"], ["b", "y"]]
>>> ohe = OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False,
...                      handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=2).fit(X)
>>> with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
...     warnings.simplefilter("always")
...     ohe.transform([["unknown_a", "unknown_b"]])
...     [str(x.message) for x in w]
["Found unknown categories in columns [1] during transform. These unknown categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.",
 "Found unknown categories in columns [0] during transform. These unknown categories will be encoded as all zeros."]
```

While fixing this I found the same inaccuracy also shows up when infrequent-category grouping isn't enabled at all (no `min_frequency`/`max_categories`, just `drop` set) — several existing tests (`test_ohe_handle_unknown_warn`, `test_ohe_drop_first_handle_unknown_ignore_warns`, `test_ohe_drop_if_binary_handle_unknown_ignore_warns`, `test_ohe_drop_first_explicit_categories`) asserted the old "infrequent category" wording even though the actual transform output was all zeros in those cases. I updated those to assert the correct "all zeros" message, and added a dedicated non-regression test for the mixed-column case from this issue.

Full diff, tests passing locally (`pytest sklearn/preprocessing/tests/test_encoders.py` — 266 passed, plus the OneHotEncoder common estimator checks):
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/compare/main...ammar-iitm:scikit-learn:fix/ohe-unknown-warning-infrequent-vs-zeros

I saw @sundeep8967 also has a fix prepared — happy to defer / compare approaches, just sharing this in case it's useful. Let me know if a formal PR from this branch would be welcome.

title: [Security] tarfile.extractall without member validation allows path traversal escape in older Python versions
body:
**Severity**: HIGH (Bandit B202)
**File**: `sklearn/utils/fixes.py`

## Vulnerability

`tarfile.extractall()` without member validation allows path traversal (zip slip). A malicious archive can write files outside the target directory.

## Fix

```python
import os

SAFE_ID = __import__("re").compile(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+$")

def _is_within_directory(directory, target):
    abs_directory = os.path.realpath(directory)
    abs_target = os.path.realpath(target)
    return abs_target.startswith(abs_directory + os.sep) or abs_target == abs_directory

def safe_extract(tar, path=".", members=None, *, numeric_owner=False):
    for member in tar.getmembers():
        member_path = os.path.join(path, member.name)
        if not _is_within_directory(path, member_path):
            raise Exception(f"Path traversal in tar: {member.name}")
    tar.extractall(path, members, numeric_owner=numeric_owner)
```

## References
- CWE-22: Path Traversal
- Bandit B202
- [OWASP: Zip Slip](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Zip_Slip)
author: sudabg

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
I think the risk of this attack is low as we only untar files from known, fixed URLs. We will also keep retiring old versions of Python when the `filter="data"` protection will come in for all users. I would be ok with implementing a fix that prevent path traversal. This isn't equivalent to the `filter="data"` but gets us a long way there. In the "detail" below a implementation of (almost) what the data filter in CPython does (direct and unchecked from AI). I am not sure doing that is worth it.
Details

```python import os import stat import tarfile def _validate_tar_members(tar, dest_path): """Backport of tarfile's filter='data' safety checks for Python < 3.12. Validates all members and returns a list of safe-to-extract members with sanitized names. """ dest_path = os.path.realpath(dest_path) safe_members = [] for member in tar.getmembers(): name = member.name # Strip leading / and os.sep if name.startswith(("/", os.sep)): name = name.lstrip("/" + os.sep) if os.path.isabs(name): raise ValueError( f"Tar member {name!r} has an absolute path" ) # Ensure extraction stays within dest_path target_path = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(dest_path, name)) if os.path.commonpath([target_path, dest_path]) != dest_path: raise ValueError( f"Tar member {name!r} would extract to {target_path!r}, " f"which is outside the destination {dest_path!r}" ) # Reject special file types (devices, FIFOs) if not (member.isreg() or member.isdir() or member.issym() or member.islnk()): raise ValueError( f"Tar member {name!r} is a special file type" ) # Validate symlink/hardlink targets if member.islnk() or member.issym(): if os.path.isabs(member.linkname): raise ValueError( f"Tar member {name!r} links to absolute path " f"{member.linkname!r}" ) if member.issym(): link_target = os.path.join( dest_path, os.path.dirname(name), member.linkname ) else: link_target = os.path.join(dest_path, member.linkname) link_target = os.path.realpath(link_target) if os.path.commonpath([link_target, dest_path]) != dest_path: raise ValueError( f"Tar member {name!r} links to {link_target!r}, " f"which is outside the destination {dest_path!r}" ) safe_members.append(member) return safe_members def tarfile_extractall(tarfile, path): try: tarfile.extractall(path, filter="data") except TypeError: _validate_tar_members(tarfile, path) tarfile.extractall(path) ```

comments.author: dunkin-dee
comments.body:
Hi, I'd like to take this on.

I've reviewed the existing `tarfile_extractall` in `sklearn/utils/fixes.py` and the issue is specifically in the `except TypeError` fallback (line 350) 
On Python < 3.12 it calls `tarfile.extractall(path)` with no member validation at all. The call sites in `_lfw.py` and `_twenty_newsgroups.py` already use `tarfile_extractall`, so no changes are needed there.

My plan is to add a `_validate_tar_members` helper (like the AI produced one) that backports the path-safety checks from CPython's `_get_filtered_attrs` in `Lib/tarfile.py`, then call it in the fallback branch before extraction. I based this on the implementation you posted, with one small correction:

- The `safe_members` list was built and returned but never passed to `extractall` as a `members=` argument. I've removed it.
- Removed the stat import

The checks I'd include:
- Strip leading slashes, then reject any remaining absolute paths
- Destination boundary check via `os.path.commonpath` (core zip-slip prevention)
- Special file rejection (devices, FIFOs)
- Symlink and hardlink target boundary validation

I'd intentionally omit permission and ownership stripping.

Does this go along with what you had in mind?

title: HTML rendering of estimator parameters does not escape potential HTML tags
body: ### Describe the bug if the docstring of a paramter contains something that could be an HTML tag it may mess up the rendering of the HTML parameter doc string We have a `t_r` attribute whose docstring contains a `` (linking to a glossary etry) which does not play well in the middle of an HTML table. ```rst t_r : :obj:`float` or :obj:`int` or None, default=None :term:`Repetition time`, in seconds (sampling period). Set to `None` if not provided. ``` ### Steps/Code to Reproduce install nilearn and make sure that you use sklearn>=1.8.0 ``` pip install nilearn scikit-learn==1.8.0 ``` run the following in a notebook (only tried on marimo) ```python from nilearn.maskers import NiftiMasker from packaging.version import parse from nilearn._version import __version__ import itertools def _doc_link_template(estimator): version_url = "dev" nil_version = parse(__version__) if nil_version.dev is None: version_url = ( f"{nil_version.major}.{nil_version.minor}.{nil_version.minor}" ) estimator_name = estimator.__class__.__name__ tmp = list( itertools.takewhile( lambda part: not part.startswith("_"), estimator.__class__.__module__.split("."), ) ) estimator_module = ".".join([tmp[0], tmp[1]]) return ( f"https://nilearn.github.io/{version_url}/modules/generated/" "{estimator_module}.{estimator_name}.html" ) masker = NiftiMasker() masker._doc_link_module = "nilearn" masker._doc_link_template = _doc_link_template(masker) masker ``` ### Expected Results a nicely laid out table ### Actual Results ### Versions ```shell sklearn 1.8.0 ```
author: Remi-Gau

title: MLPClassifier with early_stopping=True crashes on string labels: "ufunc 'isnan' not supported"
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`MLPClassifier` with `early_stopping=True` raises a `TypeError` when target labels are strings. The error originates from `_score_with_function` in `_multilayer_perceptron.py`, where `np.isnan(y_pred)` is called on predictions that have been converted back to string dtype.  
  
With `early_stopping=False`, string labels work fine. With `early_stopping=True` and numerically encoded labels, it also works fine. The issue is specifically the combination of `early_stopping=True` + string labels.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python  
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier  
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification  
import numpy as np  
  
X, y_numeric = make_classification(n_samples=200, n_features=10, n_classes=3,  
                                    n_informative=5, random_state=42)  
  
label_map = {0: "Class_A", 1: "Class_B", 2: "Class_C"}  
y_string = np.array([label_map[i] for i in y_numeric])  
  
mlp = MLPClassifier(early_stopping=True, max_iter=50, random_state=42)  
mlp.fit(X, y_string)  
```  

### Expected Results

`MLPClassifier` should handle string labels with `early_stopping=True`, just as it does with `early_stopping=False`.

Looking at the code, the plausible reason that these tests are failing is that the `estimator` object is persistent both sequentially in time (across different tests) but also used and potentially mutated _concurrently_ by multiple tests in the `--parallel-threads` case. My hypothesis is therefore that copying the estimator before running the test should solve the problems, because no mutable state will then been modified.

Unfortunately I've failed to reproduce anything locally, so I'm going to open a draft PR with this proposed fix and try a bunch of runs to see if it empirically seems to make the problem go away.

title: ENH: Improve error messages when train_size + test_size is invalid
body:
### Current Problem

When users pass invalid `test_size` / `train_size` combinations to `train_test_split` or `ShuffleSplit` (e.g. sum > 1.0, negative values, or too large numbers), the error messages from `_validate_shuffle_split` are correct but not very user-friendly.

### Proposed Improvement

Make the error messages clearer and more actionable, for example:
- Suggest valid ranges
- Give a concrete example ("try test_size=0.25 instead of 1.5")
- Clearly explain the relationship between `train_size` and `test_size`

**Location**:  
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` → `_validate_shuffle_split` function and `train_test_split`

This is a small user-experience improvement. I would like to work on it once triaged.

title: Check `column_or_1d` doesn't accept `StringDType` as `dtype` parameter  since Pandas 3
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Since Pandas 3.0, `StringDType` is not anymore a valid Numpy data type. This makes `check_column_or_1d` crash when called with that type as `dtype` parameter.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.utils.validation import column_or_1d
import pandas as pd
pd.options.future.infer_string = True # So this test also works in the 2.x series also


df = pd.DataFrame({"y": ["a", "b", "a", "c"]})
column_or_1d(df["y"], dtype=df["y"].dtype) # fails
```

### Expected Results

No error is thrown.

### Actual Results

```

comments.author: repeating
comments.body:
hey, i dug into this one — the root cause is that `check_array` tries to call `np.dtype(dtype)` on whatever you pass in, but pandas 3's `StringDtype` has no numpy equivalent so it throws a `TypeError`. the other nullable extension types (`Int64Dtype`, `Float64Dtype`, etc.) are handled earlier in the pipeline, but `StringDtype` slips through to that line.

fix is a small try/except around the `np.dtype()` call — if it raises `TypeError`, reset `dtype=None` and let numpy figure out the natural dtype (which ends up being `object` for string data, same as before pandas 3).

opening a PR now.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
That's because pandas 3's `StringDtype` is not a numpy dtype subclass (nor a valid value to pass to `numpy.astype`).

To me the `dtype` argument passed to `check_array` or `column_or_1d` should be the dtype of the resulting NumPy array since the point of `check_array` is to try its best of taking a polymorphing input and turn it into a valid numpy array with the requested dtype. Since it's not possible to create a numpy array with `pandas.StringDType` (independently of scikit-learn), I don't see the point in changing `check_array` to pretend that it's the case.

For the same reason, I would expect the following to fail:

```python
from sklearn.utils.validation import column_or_1d
import pandas as pd

column_or_1d([1, 2, 3], dtype=pd.Int32Dtype())
```

while the following should work:

```python
column_or_1d([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.int32)
```

title: PytestRemovedIn10Warning (pytest version 9.1.1.) with sklearn parametrize_with_checks
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

The recent pytest update (9.1.1) introduces a warning in our scikit-learn compatibility tests for our own encoders. Our encoder inherits from scikit-learn’s `TransformerMixin` and `BaseEstimator`, and we use `sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.parametrize_with_checks` to verify that the custom encoders are compatible with scikit-learn.

The warning originates from `parametrize_with_checks`, which essentially returns a `pytest.mark.parametrize`. It currently passes a generator to `pytest.mark.parametrize`. However, this is deprecated in current versions of pytest.

It would therefore be useful to review or update the `parametrize_with_checks` implementation so that it no longer relies on the deprecated generator behavior. This will allow us in the future to keep testing for scikit-learn compatibility.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Run the following file using pytest's latest version (9.1.1):

```python
import pytest
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import parametrize_with_checks


@parametrize_with_checks([DummyRegressor()])
def test(estimator, check):
    check(estimator)
```

This can be run from terminal with `pytest name_of_file.py`


### Expected Results

The expected result is no warning about deprecation from pytest.

### Actual Results

```
PytestRemovedIn10Warning: Passing a non-Collection iterable to parametrize is deprecated.
Test: LOCATION, argvalues type: generator
Please convert to a list or tuple.
See https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/deprecations.html#parametrize-iterators
metafunc.parametrize(*marker.args, **marker.kwargs, _param_mark=marker)
```

    num_threads: 4

        version: 0.3.33.112.0

### Interest in fixing the bug

The fix seems relatively easy.
The link in the warning provides a solution: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/deprecations.html#parametrize-iterators

As such, we could wrap the return generator in a list like:

```python
return pytest.mark.parametrize(
        "estimator, check",
        list(_checks_generator(estimators, legacy, expected_failed_checks)),
        ids=_get_check_estimator_ids,
    )
```

I'm glad there was a fix quickly applied, but I suspect that once a `pytest` 10.x comes out changing this warning to an error, it might cause problems for projects that try to stay compatible with a wide range of `scikit-learn` versions (since the fix will presumably only be in the next version, `>1.9.0`).

In case it's helpful to anyone finding this issue from search in the future... here's how we're attempting to maintain backwards and forwards compatibility with both `scikit-learn` and `pytest` in LightGBM's tests:

```python
from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import parametrize_with_checks as sklearn_parametrize_with_checks


def parametrize_with_checks(estimator, *args, **kwargs):
    mark_decorator = sklearn_parametrize_with_checks(estimator, *args, **kwargs)
    argnames, argvalues = mark_decorator.args
    return pytest.mark.parametrize(argnames, list(argvalues), **mark_decorator.kwargs)

@parametrize_with_checks(
    [lgb.LGBMClassifier(), lgb.LGBMRegressor()],
    expected_failed_checks=_get_expected_failed_tests,
)
def test_sklearn_integration(estimator, check):
    estimator.set_params(min_child_samples=1, min_data_in_bin=1)
    check(estimator)
```

body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

The ColumnTransformer lets you pick a subset of columns to apply transformers to (or to keep or drop). I find this immensely useful in my day to day work, since it makes complex featurization pipelines a lot more maintainable.

One speedbump I keep running into is the error messaging when columns are missing. Let's dissect this example, where I make a dataframe and try to access two columns which are not present:
```python
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Foo":[1,2,3,4],
    "Bar": [5,6,7,8]
})
transformer = ColumnTransformer([
    ("Foo Transformer", "passthrough", ["Foo", 
                                        "Missing Column 1", 
                                        "Missing Column 2"]),
    ("Bar Transformer", "passthrough", ["Bar"]),
]).set_output(transform="pandas")
transformer.fit_transform(df)
```

Truncating the traceback a little bit to the relevant parts:
```
...
File ~\miniconda3\envs\sklearn\lib\site-packages\pandas\core\indexes\base.py:3812, in Index.get_loc(self, key)
   3811         raise InvalidIndexError(key)
-> 3812     raise KeyError(key) from err
   3813 except TypeError:
   3814     # If we have a listlike key, _check_indexing_error will raise
   3815     #  InvalidIndexError. Otherwise we fall through and re-raise
   3816     #  the TypeError.

KeyError: 'Missing Column 1'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

<more output here>

File ~\miniconda3\envs\sklearn\lib\site-packages\sklearn\utils\_indexing.py:451, in _get_column_indices(X, key)
    448         column_indices.append(col_idx)
    450 except KeyError as e:
--> 451     raise ValueError("A given column is not a column of the dataframe") from e
    453 return column_indices

ValueError: A given column is not a column of the dataframe
```

Although the Pandas traceback catches the first missing column ("Missing Column 1"), it ends there. Then we kick back over to sklearn, who notices the key error and informs us.

This may seem like it's easily solvable (e.g. "Just check your columns first!"), but it ends up being incredibly difficult to debug once you're in a deep pipeline with 2-3 transformation steps, themselves potentially going into nested column transformers and pipelines. Throw in custom classes that also rename your columns, and more than 1-2 misnamed/missing features, and it becomes very time consuming.

### Describe your proposed solution

It would be a huge quality of life improvement to list all columns which are causing the key-error, instead of just the first.
Normally I address this by just patching my copy of sklearn in `sklearn/utils/_indexing.py`. Around line 450 in `_get_column_indices`:
```python
        except KeyError as e:
            missing = {*columns} - {*all_columns}
            raise ValueError(
                f"A given column is not a column of the dataframe: {missing}"
            ) from e
```
Which yields this more informative traceback:
```
File ~\miniconda3\envs\sklearn\lib\site-packages\sklearn\utils\_indexing.py:452, in _get_column_indices(X, key)
    450 except KeyError as e:
    451     missing = {*columns} - {*all_columns}
--> 452     raise ValueError(
    453         f"A given column is not a column of the dataframe: {missing}"
    454     ) from e
    456 return column_indices

ValueError: A given column is not a column of the dataframe: {'Missing Column 1', 'Missing Column 2'}
```
Looks like a similar approach might be usable to modify the `get_column_indices_interchange` function a few lines down, but I haven't tested this on it.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

See above manual patching (certainly not the best solution however)

### Additional context

I am willing to have a go at making this PR if you'd like!

title: FeatureUnion with polars output fails due to missing column renaming in adapter interface

### Describe the bug

When using `FeatureUnion` with `set_config(transform_output="polars")`, the operation fails with `polars.exceptions.DuplicateError` because the `ContainerAdapterProtocol.hstack()` interface is incomplete - it doesn't accept `feature_names` parameter to apply column renaming before concatenation.

from sklearn.pipeline import FeatureUnion
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn import set_config
import numpy as np

union = FeatureUnion([

    ("scaler2", StandardScaler())
])
result = union.fit_transform(X)

comments.author: Akarashak51
comments.body:
### Root Cause Analysis

The issue stems from an implicit array conversion in the LBFGS solver path when processing DPNP arrays. Based on the error `TypeError: Implicit conversion to a NumPy array is not allowed. Please use '.asnumpy()' to construct a NumPy array`, this occurs because:

1. **Array API Dispatch Chain**: When `array_api_dispatch=True`, scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression` should maintain array API compatibility throughout the computation pipeline, but the LBFGS solver internally attempts to convert DPNP arrays to NumPy without going through proper Array API namespace functions.

2. **Solver-Specific Handling**: The `_logistic_regression_path` function in `sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py` likely calls `scipy.optimize.minimize` with LBFGS, which expects NumPy arrays. The conversion layer between Array API and scipy's optimizer is where the implicit conversion fails for DPNP.

### Proposed Solutions

**Option 1: Explicit Array API → NumPy Conversion Layer**
- Add a conversion wrapper in `_logistic_regression_path` that detects Array API arrays and converts them explicitly before passing to scipy
- Use `array_namespace()` to get the namespace, then convert via the proper API
- Ensures LBFGS path works with all Array API backends

**Option 2: Extend Array API Support in Solver**
- Implement LBFGS optimization using Array API primitives directly
- Similar to how `newton-cg` and `lbfgs` solvers could be refactored to use `array_api_compat` functions
- More complex but provides native Array API support

**Option 3: Backend-Specific Fallback**
- Detect DPNP arrays specifically and use `.asnumpy()` to convert to NumPy before optimization
- Process results and convert back to DPNP after fitting
- Quick fix but less elegant than proper Array API integration

### Implementation Strategy

I'd recommend **Option 1** as the most pragmatic approach:

```python
# In sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace

def _check_solver_for_array_api(X, y, solver):
    xp, is_array_api = get_namespace(X, y)
    
    if is_array_api and solver in ['lbfgs', 'newton-cg']:
        # Convert to NumPy for scipy-based solvers
        import numpy as np
        X_np = np.asarray(X)
        y_np = np.asarray(y)
        return X_np, y_np, xp
    return X, y, None

# Then in _logistic_regression_path:
# X_work, y_work, original_namespace = _check_solver_for_array_api(X, y, solver)
# ... perform optimization ...
# if original_namespace is not None:
#     coef_ = original_namespace.asarray(coef_)
```

### Testing Approach

- Add DPNP-specific tests in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_logistic.py`
- Test with both CPU and GPU devices if available
- Verify coefficient accuracy matches NumPy baseline
- Ensure gradient computations remain consistent

### Edge Cases to Consider

1. **Multi-class classification**: Ensure one-vs-rest and multinomial modes work
2. **Warm start**: Verify `warm_start=True` handles array conversions correctly
3. **Sample weights**: Check `sample_weight` parameter conversion
4. **Sparse arrays**: Confirm sparse DPNP arrays (if supported) don't break

I'd be happy to help validate any fix through testing, especially around numerical consistency between DPNP and NumPy backends.

title: clone: treat class-valued parameters as non-estimators (avoid TypeError) [swev-id: scikit-learn__scikit-learn-12585]
body:
## User request
Clone fails for parameters that are estimator types.

Key: clone should not error when a parameter is a class; adjust clone to treat classes as non-estimators (e.g., check isinstance(estimator, type) or ismethod(get_params)).

## Research specification
- Location: sklearn/base.py, function `clone`.
- Problem: When an estimator has a parameter whose value is a class/type (e.g., `LogisticRegression` rather than an instance), `clone` attempts to call `get_params` on the class object, leading to `TypeError: get_params() missing 1 required positional argument: 'self'`.
- Proposed change: Add an early guard in `clone` after container-type handling:
  - `elif isinstance(estimator, type): return estimator`
  - Treat Python classes/types as non-estimators and leave them unchanged, both at top level and within parameter traversal.
- Edge cases:
  - Estimator parameter set to a scikit-learn estimator class → preserved unchanged.
  - Parameter set to a user-defined class type (not `BaseEstimator`) → preserved unchanged.
  - numpy scalar types (e.g., `np.float64`) → preserved unchanged as types.
  - typing/dataclass types → preserved unchanged.
- Tests:
  - New tests to ensure cloning succeeds and preserves identity for class-valued parameters; estimator instances continue to be cloned.
- Risk & API consistency:
  - Minimal, backward-compatible change; relaxes previous erroneous behavior when encountering class objects. Normal estimator instance cloning behavior is unchanged.
author: rowan-stein

comments.author: Mohataseem89
comments.body:
thanks for reporting this issue

I can reproduce the problem: `clone` treats class-valued parameters as estimators and attempts to call `get_params` on them, which raises a `TypeError`.

I would like to work on this by updating `sklearn.base.clone` to treat Python classes `(isinstance(obj, type))` as non-estimators and return them unchanged, both at top level and when encountered as parameter values. I’ll also add tests to ensure class-valued parameters are preserved while estimator instances continue to be cloned correctly

title: [BUG] Partial dependence integer-feature deprecation message references outdated version (1.9)
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

## Summary

`sklearn/inspection/_partial_dependence.py` around line 720 still
emits a `FutureWarning` stating that integer-valued feature inputs
"will raise ValueError in scikit-learn 1.9". scikit-learn 1.9 has
passed, so the warning message is stale and the behavior has not
been updated to match the original intent.

## Current behavior

Passing integer feature indices to `partial_dependence()` emits:
```
FutureWarning: ... will raise a ValueError in scikit-learn 1.9
```

## Expected behavior

Either:
1. The behavior raises `ValueError` as originally promised (the
   deprecation endpoint is enforced), or
2. The deprecation period has been extended and the message is
   updated to reference the correct future version

## Files affected

- `sklearn/inspection/_partial_dependence.py` (~line 720)
- `sklearn/inspection/tests/test_partial_dependence.py`
- Possibly one user guide page if it documents this warning

## Question for maintainers

Was the ValueError enforcement intentionally deferred beyond 1.9?
If so, what is the target version? I'd like to implement the fix
once the intended end-state is confirmed — I don't want to enforce
the error if the timeline was quietly extended.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

import numpy as np
import warnings
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence

X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6], [7, 8]])
y = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1])

model = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=10, random_state=0)
model.fit(X, y)

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    partial_dependence(model, X, features=[0])
    for warning in w:
        print(warning.category.__name__, ":", warning.message)
```

### Expected Results


**Expected Results**
```
One of two consistent outcomes:

1. If the deprecation endpoint has been reached: a ValueError is raised
   for integer-valued feature inputs, as originally promised in the
   warning message.

2. If the deprecation period was extended: the FutureWarning message
   references the correct future version, not the already-passed 1.9.

Either way, the current message should not reference a version that
has already been released.
```

### Actual Results


**Actual Results**
```
A FutureWarning is emitted referencing scikit-learn 1.9, which has
already been released:

FutureWarning: ... will raise a ValueError in scikit-learn 1.9

The warning message is stale — scikit-learn 1.9 has passed but
the behavior has not changed. Users following this warning will
expect an error that never comes, eroding trust in the deprecation
process.

- sklearn/inspection/_partial_dependence.py (~line 720)
- sklearn/inspection/tests/test_partial_dependence.py

title: Using `move_to` on a numpy array with negative stride crashes the Python process
body:
The `move_to` function we have for moving arrays from one namespace to another can crash the Python process when you ask it to move an array with negative strides. I found this while working on `PCA` where we have an array with negative stride (`Vt` from `_fit_truncated`).

The code below is a reproducer:

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
import sklearn
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_to

def make_negative_strided():
    """A small, contiguous-source array viewed with a negative stride."""
    a = np.arange(12.0).reshape(3, 4)[:, ::-1]
    assert not a.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]
    assert a.strides[-1] < 0
    return a

a = make_negative_strided()
with sklearn.config_context(array_api_dispatch=True):
    xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(torch.asarray([1.0]))
    try:
        move_to(a, xp=xp, device=device)
    except Exception as exc:  # it is not caught
        print("Caught a Python exception (unexpected):", type(exc).__name__, exc)
    else:
        # this doesn't happen
        print("move_to returned without error (unexpected)")

    # instead the process exits with a SIGABRT
```

AI tells me that a possible fix is to call `np.ascontiguousarray(array)` if the input `array` is an array with negative stride. In addition we should [only apply this workaround in the case where the `move_to` target is torch](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34307#issuecomment-4778962780). The comment for the workaround should also include a link to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/188023 and this issue so we can know when the work around can be removed.

Something like this, but with a check for torch as target:
```diff
--- a/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
+++ b/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
@@ def move_to(*arrays, xp, device):
             xp_array, _, device_array = get_namespace_and_device(array)
             if xp == xp_array and device == device_array:
                 converted_arrays.append(array)
             else:
+                strides = getattr(array, "strides", None)
+                if strides is not None and any(
+                    stride < 0 for stride in strides
+                ):
+                    # Some libraries (e.g. torch) do not raise a catchable
+                    # Python exception but abort the whole process when a NumPy
+                    # array with negative or zero strides is imported via DLPack
+                    # (such arrays are produced for instance by ``a[::-1]``
+                    # reversals, as done by ARPACK). The ``except`` clause below
+                    # therefore cannot protect against it, so the source array is
+                    # made contiguous first to guarantee positive strides.
+                    array = numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)
                 try:
                     # The dlpack protocol is the future proof and library agnostic
                     # method to transfer arrays across namespace and device boundaries
                     # hence this method is attempted first and going through NumPy is
                     # only used as fallback in case of failure.
                     # Note: copy=None is the default since array-api 2023.12. Namespace
                     # libraries should only trigger a copy automatically if needed.
                     array_converted = xp.from_dlpack(array, device=device)
```

What do others think about this? I am also wondering if this is a bug in numpy's DLPack implementation (should not expose arrays with negative stride) or if this is a bug in torch (should check for negative stride before doing anything)?

I think that `numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)` is free for most arrays, those that already full fill it. For arrays that are not already contiguous I don't know what the cost is, but I think there is no alternative?

I can reproduce this and tested a small local fix.

My understanding is that the guard needs to happen before the DLPack path, because PyTorch can abort the process before Python can catch an exception. The fix I tested only materializes NumPy arrays with negative strides via `numpy.ascontiguousarray` before calling `xp.from_dlpack`; other arrays keep the existing path.

I also added a subprocess regression test so a failure cannot abort the pytest worker.

Would this be an acceptable direction? If yes, I can open a focused PR with the fix and test.

[scikit-learn’s array API support is limited to NumPy, CuPy, and PyTorch](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/modules/array_api.html). Since Pandas is not one of them, the behaviour you observed is expected.

Closing as not a bug.</s>

Edit: See https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/33822#issuecomment-4297072468.

comments.author: lorentzenchr
comments.body: @virchan Don‘t you find the error message cryptic?

comments.author: david-cortes-intel
comments.body:
@virchan Thanks for your quick response. This detail is very unclear from the documentation for array API, and it's not obvious to me from what one can find throughout this issue tracker that it is the intended design either (e.g. https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/32836 https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28668#issuecomment-2785250616)

Would be very helpful if the docs could describe in more details these compatibility constraints.

comments.author: virchan
comments.body: > [@virchan](https://github.com/virchan) Don‘t you find the error message cryptic? I don't, but that's probably because I've become numb after working on Array API support for a while and, as a result, overlooked the user's point of view 😅. But I see your point now, @david-cortes-intel. The [move_to](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/199b55ec0620e2ddd034a75ac0ebd5f4e5e9c946/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py#L523) function should be able to move Pandas dataframe to the reference array type, since we consider it as NumPy compat namespace in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32838. Reopening the issue, and apologies for the noise.

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
I'm not sure if we should start accepting `pd.Series` and converting it for the user. The reason I am a bit hesitant is that once we start allowing it, we can't easily go back to not accepting it. This is what makes me want to ponder this for a bit.

For example, I think we should not get in a situation where it looks like `move_to(X_df, ..)` would work. I think when `X` is a data frame we should take the "not array API" path through the scikit-learn code and not trigger a conversion of it to Numpy.

The reason I bring up moving `X` is that it feels like that is an edge case we should consider in the decision of how all this should work.

A reason to support converting a `y = pd.Series()` for the user is that I think you can pass `y = list()` and we convert that too. Even though a `list` isn't a array API thing.

---

We should update the documentation and improve the error messages. No matter if we decide to accept `pd.Series` there will always be things that we do not accept, so having a good error message seems like a good thing.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: I think we can/should accept `pd.Series` when it has a numerical dtype (but fail otherwise, as for a numpy array with str or object dtype).

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
I think this particular problem can be fixed by:

```python
diff --git a/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py b/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
index 0819c94912..1fbedd2c81 100644
--- a/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
+++ b/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
@@ -613,6 +613,7 @@ def move_to(*arrays, xp, device):
                     # TODO: ValueError not needed once min NumPy >=2.4.0:
                     # https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/30341
                 except (
+                    AssertionError,
                     AttributeError,
                     TypeError,
                     NotImplementedError,
```

but I am not sure this is the correct way to fix this.

comments.author: david-cortes-intel
comments.body:
> I think we can/should accept `pd.Series` when it has a numerical dtype (but fail otherwise, as for a numpy array with str or object dtype).

But classifiers do accept string types.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: Indeed, there is a problem in the way we do things. I think we should not try to move `y_true` when it holds non-numeric content in classification metrics. Instead, we should move the result of label encoding / one-hot / ordinal encoding of the class labels into boolean or integer class membership indicators just before they are combined with `y_pred` and `sample_weight` using the namespace / device / dtype of `y_pred`. The details of how this happens is specific for each classification metric I believe.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: Note that there is a related fix in #34065 to make `RidgeClassifier.fit` pass the common tests for mixed input namespaces, but that does not fix the problem with `.score`. We probably need to improve the common test to cover this.

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
I can see how from a user's perspective, one might expect a pandas series or df to comply to the array API rules, since we did not document otherwise and pandas input is usually converted to numpy in the process (in `check_array`). Thanks for reporting that, @david-cortes-intel.

But in array API we are explicitly excluding pandas from being an array namespace. In `_remove_non_arrays` (called in `get_namespace_and_device`), we filter out dataframe inputs:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/0f0ff8cfb19c6dd9ec64ac6b96f36437f0e0720e/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py#L350-L351

Therefore, and because we are planning to support narwhals, I think it is better not to take pandas objects under the umbrella of `array_api_dispatch=True` right now (which in my mind would be a new feature).

I would suggest two actions:
1) document cleanly that we don't consider dataframe inputs as array containers
2) catch the torch error and re-raise it with a clearer scikit-learn message

CC, @AnneBeyer, because this issue is a good starting point for thinking about the scope of array API, if you are interested to participate.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
I find it unexpected that `model.score(X, y)` would accept y as a pandas series when `array_api_dispatch=False` but would raise an exception when `array_api_dispatch=True`.

The goal is to enable array API dispatch by default in the future, we should not introduce a usability regression when doing so.

I think we need to find a way to change to ensure that `model.fit(X, y)` and `model.score(X, y)` still accept pandas dataframes and series whether array API dispatch is enabled or not.

Since when array API dispatch is disabled, this particular estimator treats pandas series as array-like and converts them to NumPy array, we should continue doing so here.

Other estimators such as `ColumnTransformer` have particular handling of pandas dataframes, and we should ensure that we do not break that.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: I think this is a bug to me, and we probably need to extend the common test discussed in #34094 to cover non-array API array-like inputs (in particular dataframes and series).

title: Inconsistent type of predictions and `classes_` for array API classifiers
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

There's currently 2 classifiers with array API support:
* `LogisticRegression`
* `RidgeClassifier`

The docs and discussions in this issue tracker are quite unclear about what should be the expected behavior when input types are mixed in the case of classifiers.

Since in general 'y' can be something like strings or non-sequential integers that get re-encoded internally, I think it makes sense that the `classes_` attributes under array API would be obtained from the type of 'y' and then sliced when returning something from `.predict()` - i.e. "prediction follows 'y'".

This appears to be the case for `LogisticRegression`:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
import torch

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.random(size=(20,3))
y = rng.integers(2, size=X.shape[0])
yt = torch.tensor(y, device="xpu", dtype=torch.float32)

from sklearn import set_config
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)
model = LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs").fit(X, yt)
model.classes_
```
```
tensor([0., 1.], device='xpu:0')
```

But the docs state "everything follows 'X'" instead, and `RidgeClassifier` does appear to follow this logic from the docs, even if it might not be as natural for classification scenarios:
```python
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
model = RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(X, yt)
model.classes_
```
```
array([0., 1.], dtype=float32)
```

Described above.

All classifiers with array API support should work like in `LogisticRegression`.

`RidgeClassifier` works differently.

title: Handling of classes with all-zero weights
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

If passing multi-class data to a classifier where some class has only observations with zero weights, estimators will produce odd solutions which do not really make sense.

For example:
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.random(size=(30, 3))
y = rng.integers(3, size=X.shape[0])
w = rng.standard_gamma(1, size=X.shape[0])
w[y == 1] = 0.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
LogisticRegression().fit(X, y, w).coef_
```
```
array([[-0.01295201,  0.04689646, -0.19975591],
       [ 0.0006037 ,  0.00044906,  0.00039081],
       [ 0.01234832, -0.04734552,  0.19936509]])
```

Mathematically, the correct solution would be something with a minus infinite as intercept and zeros in all coefficients, and the same applies to other classifiers with intercepts (e.g. gradient boosters), but I don't think this would be a desirable solution.

Technically, the sample weights according to the documentation should be interpreted as if each observation would be repeated the amount of times given by the weights, and if we take that as zero, that means leaving them out, in which case the classes with zero weights would be removed during the pre-processing and would not be available under `model.classes_`.

But that sort of behavior would be quite problematic for other libraries that aim at providing scikit-learn-compatible interfaces - for example, it'd contradict the docs that instruct developers to call `np.unique` to get the classes ([link](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#estimator-types)), and if implemented in such a way that [validate_data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.utils.validation.validate_data.html) could return something with different shape than the input, it might require other scikit-learn-compatible libraries to have a hard dependency on scikit-learn, and would likely break many things if the shapes differ.

Thus, I think the most reasonable behavior here would be to error out with an informative message.

For reference, this is what GLMNET would do, and would even have a non-zero threshold for it which is perhaps a more reasonable way of handling it:
```r
library(glmnet)
data("iris")
x <- iris[, -5]
y <- iris$Species
w <- rep(1, length(y))
w[y == "virginica"] <- 0
glmnet(x, y, weights=w, family="multinomial")
```
```
Error: from glmnet C++ code (error code 8003); Null probability for class 3 < 1.0e-5
```

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Reproducer given above.

### Expected Results

In order of preference, should either:
* Error out; or
* Filter out the classes; or
* Produce a mathematically correct solution.

### Actual Results

Produces an incorrect solution.

### Versions

```shell
Not relevant.
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No.
author: david-cortes

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
Thanks for pointing us to that, @david-cortes.

We already have #16298 for incorrect `sample_weight` handling which is an ongoing meta-issue. `LogisticRegression` specifically is on that list.

When an entire class being filtered out breaks downstream dependencies, this seems like a valid concern.

Highlighting the following passages, because they shed a light from the perspective of other libraries on `sample_weight` handling in scikit-learn estimators:

>Technically, the sample weights according to the documentation should be interpreted as if each observation would be repeated the amount of times given by the weights, and if we take that as zero, that means leaving them out, in which case the classes with zero weights would be removed during the pre-processing and would not be available under model.classes_.

> But that sort of behavior would be quite problematic for other libraries that aim at providing scikit-learn-compatible interfaces - for example, it'd contradict the docs that instruct developers to call np.unique to get the classes ([link](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#estimator-types)), and if implemented in such a way that [validate_data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.utils.validation.validate_data.html) could return something with different shape than the input, it might require other scikit-learn-compatible libraries to have a hard dependency on scikit-learn, and would likely break many things if the shapes differ.

> Thus, I think the most reasonable behavior here would be to error out with an informative message.

Do you think that defining `estimator.classes_ = np.unique(y)` while still fitting without zero-weight samples is an option?

Is there a common use case where all the samples of one class get filtered out but the user may still be interested in predictions, that would make raising an error the wrong choice for these cases? (Is warm starting such a thing? Or if users define as certain class for invalid samples?)

CC: @ogrisel, @snath-xoc, @antoinebaker

comments.author: david-cortes
comments.body:
> Do you think that defining estimator.classes_ = np.unique(y) while still fitting without zero-weight samples is an option?

But how would that work out? For example, in LogisticRegression, the coefficients have a shape given by the number of classes, so you cannot leave classes without coefficients.

> Is there a common use case where all the samples of one class get filtered out but the user may still be interested in predictions

It can happen if weights are determined by some other method, like bias-correcting procedures; or if they come frome some boostrapping process where observations are given a weight instead of subsetting the data, among others. But in those particular cases, a situation where some class ends up with a weight of zero would have to be an error in the higher-level procedure.

comments.author: lorentzenchr
comments.body:
Note that `LogisticRegression` uses an L2-penalty by default (`C=1`, see #28711 if you would prefer a penalty alpha instead of the anti-penalty C). This penalty acts like a Baysian prior. The less data you have, the more you rely on the prior.
Secondly, note that the multinomial loss couples the coefficients of different classes.

If you specify a tiny penalty, you get
```python
LogisticRegression(C=np.inf).fit(X, y, w).coef_
# array([[ 1.1845094 ,  0.98248565,  0.54307125],
#        [-2.78259988, -1.60964584, -2.3640526 ],  <- this is now all negative
#        [ 1.59809049,  0.62716019,  1.82098135]])
```
Without penalty, we are free add a constant to the feature coefficients of each class, meaning
```python
c = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf).fit(X, y, w).coef_
c - c[1, :]
# array([[3.96710928, 2.59213149, 2.90712385],
#        [0.        , 0.        , 0.        ],
#        [4.38069037, 2.23680603, 4.18503395]])
```

There are also use cases that need "no class observed" functionality, e.g., grid search.

**Summary**: There is no bug and no inconsistency.

comments.author: david-cortes
comments.body:
@lorentzenchr The intercepts are not regularized in multinomial logistic regression.

By the logic you sketched, if 'C' is non-infinite, if two solutions produce the same predicted probabilities but one has zeros in the coefficients while the other has non-zero values, then the one with zeros is more optimal. That optimal solution would be obtained with a negative-infinite intercept.

comments.author: lorentzenchr
comments.body:
> The intercepts are not regularized in multinomial logistic regression.

The intercepts are never penalized.

> if two solutions produce the same predicted probabilities but one has zeros in the coefficients while the other has non-zero values, then the one with zeros is more optimal.

No. Apart from the intercept, the optimal coefficients are the ones with minimal L2-norm (or L1-norm if you switch to that penalty). You might be interested in https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1311.6529 Chapter/Lemma 3.1.

comments.author: david-cortes
comments.body:
> Apart from the intercept, the optimal coefficients are the ones with minimal L2-norm

Yes, that's what I just mentioned. From there, if you do the math, you'll see that the solution produced by scikit-learn is suboptimal.

comments.author: david-cortes
comments.body:
If the argument is not clear, perhaps a quick numerical proof of suboptimality might help.

This is the model produced by scikit-learn:
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.random(size=(30, 3))
y = rng.integers(3, size=X.shape[0])
w = rng.standard_gamma(1, size=X.shape[0])
w[y == 1] = 0.

C = 1.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(C=C).fit(X, y, w)
```

Evaluating the objective function that it is supposed to minimize:
```python
proba = model.predict_proba(X)

from sklearn.metrics import log_loss
def fn_being_optimized(proba, y, C, coef):
    return C*log_loss(y, proba) + 0.5*np.dot(coef.reshape(-1), coef.reshape(-1))
fn_being_optimized(proba, y, C, model.coef_)
```
```
np.float64(4.830843455584648)
```

If that were the optimal solution, then it shouldn't be possible to achieve a lower number, but that can be done as follows:
```python
X_sub = X[y != 1]
y_sub = y[y != 1]
w_sub = w[y != 1]
model_sub = LogisticRegression(C=C/2).fit(X_sub, y_sub, w_sub)
coef_better = np.zeros((3, model.coef_.shape[1]))
coef_better[0] = model_sub.coef_[0]
coef_better[2] = -model_sub.coef_[0]
intercept_better = np.zeros(3)
intercept_better[0] = model_sub.intercept_[0]
intercept_better[1] = -10

from scipy.special import softmax
proba_better = softmax(
    X @ coef_better.T + intercept_better,
    axis=1
)
fn_being_optimized(proba_better, y, C, coef_better)
```
```
np.float64(4.017919827979346)
```

And if you do the math, you'll also notice that in theory the function should decrease as the $-10$ I put there approaches minus infinity.

comments.author: lorentzenchr
comments.body:
In case of doubt, change the solver to "newton-cholesky" or "newton-cg". Also note that your objective function might not be the correct one. To be sure, run
```python
LogisticRegression(C=C, solver="newton-cholesky", verbose=1).fit(X, y, w)
# Solver did converge at loss = 0.6635209912367211.

LogisticRegression(C=C, solver="newton-cg").fit(X, y, w)
# Solver did converge at loss = 0.6635902284521691.
```
That is close enough.

comments.body:
@lorentzenchr Even if the objective function does not match exactly against the formula used by scikit-learn, in the example above, the made-up solution achieves both lower log-loss and lower L2 norm of coefficients if evaluated separately. They aren't close, and you'll also see that the class predictions are different:

```

    return np.dot(x.reshape(-1), x.reshape(-1))
sqnm(model.coef_), sqnm(coef_better)
```

```python
proba.argmax(axis=1), proba_better.argmax(axis=1)

comments.author: david-cortes
comments.body: @lorentzenchr This is not a bug in any particular optimizer. The issue is about scikit-learn trying to use a numeric solver for a problem that has only non-finite optimal solutions, which can never be reached through those kinds of methods, and where the calculations would break with floating point arithmetic even if they are well defined in theory.

comments.author: lorentzenchr
comments.body:
> a problem that has only non-finite optimal solutions

Show me.

comments.author: david-cortes
comments.body:
Breaking it down to the most basic terms possible: by definition, logistic regression is meant to minimize a weighted sum of a term which is the squared L2 norm of coefficients, and another term which is the negative log-likelihood of observations:

$$
f(\beta) = c_1 \sum_{i=1}^n (w_i l_i) + c_2  \lVert \beta \rVert ^2
$$
$$
c_1 > 0
$$
$$
c_2 \geq 0
$$

The second term achieves its minimum (equal to zero) when $\beta$ is all zeros.

By the very definition of log-likelihood:

$$
l_i = - \log ( p_i(y = y_i) )
$$

So the first term asymptotically reaches zero (its minimum) as the predicted probability of the class to which an observation belongs tends towards 1.

For $k=3$ (three classes), for a single observation, denoting the linear scores as $x_1, x_2, x_3$, the predicted probability for, say, class 1, is given as:

$$
p(y = 1) = \frac{ \exp{x_1} }{ \exp{x_1} + \exp{x_2} + \exp{x_3}  }
$$

That probability increases as $x_1$ moves towards positive infinity, and as $x_2$ and $x_3$ move towards negative infinity, regardless of what the values for $x_1, x_2, x_3$ are. If that part is not clear, take the first derivatives to corroborate.

If a given class has zeros in all the observations (here that was class 2), then the predicted probabilities for that class will not play any role in the formula:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n (w_i l_i) = \sum_{i \\: s.t. w_i \neq 0} (w_i l_i)
$$

Thus, for every observation of class 1, you have that:

$$
p(y = 1 | x_2 = q - |e|) > p(y = 1 | x_2 = q)
$$

And for every observation of class 3:

$$
p(y = 3 | x_2 = q - |e|) > p(y = 3 | x_2 = q)
$$

Meaning: as $x_2$ decreases for every observation, the function being minimized will keep getting lower. This can be seen clearly in the equations, but will not play out like that in floating point numbers that don't have infinite precision.

Every $x_2$ in this case gets added the intercept for class 2, so for every possible finite-valued solution that could be obtained, a better solution could be made by lowering the intercept for the second class, which would decrease $x_2$ for every observation, thereby decreasing the first term of the initial formula without impacting the second one.

Since the regularization term reaches its minimum when all coefficients are zero, and since lower values of $x_2$ (the linear score for class 2) are more optimal for every observation, then for any possible solution where a coefficient for the second class is non-zero, a better solution could be made by adding the sum of the most negative feature-dependent linear score to the intercept and making the coefficients for that class be zero instead. And if a given feature-dependent lienar score is positive, a better solution would be obtained by making it zero instead, which would be the case for zero-valued coefficients.

Thus, a solution can only be optimal if the coefficients for the class with zero weights are all zero and its intercept is negative infinite. Otherwise, the solution could be improved by either lowering the intercept, or by trading off coefficients for intercept.

comments.author: lorentzenchr
comments.body:
Without intercept, your conclusion is not true. Without intercept, the coefficients will not be zero and among the ones producing the same probabilities the one which is class centered is best (for L2 penalty), see https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1311.6529.

The problem is only apparent with intercept. A higher tolerance makes this evident:
```python
LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky", tol=1e-15).fit(X, y, w).intercept_
# 11.86636445, -23.1304276 ,  11.26406315
```
BTW, the correct objective function is
```python
def f(X, y, w, m):
    p = m.predict_proba(X)
    return log_loss(y, p, sample_weight=w) + 1/(2*m.C*np.sum(w)) * np.linalg.norm(m.coef_, ord=2)**2
```

comments.author: david-cortes
comments.body:
> If we talk only about LogisticRegression

@lorentzenchr This is not only about logistic regression. Please read the problem description again.

> what/where is the problem (=use case that goes wrong).?

Among others:
* In cases where it works by accident, like logistic regression, it produces incorrect solutions which distort other procedures where those results might be used in aggregate. You can see in the earlier example that the coefficients from the initial solution are not close to the coefficients that would be obtained by discarding the empty class for example (those are mathematically optimal). If that were to be plugged into a bootstrapping procedure for instance, it would result in misestimating the variances, and would likewise distort other metrics if put into a cross-validator.
* It goes against what the documentation says is the interpretation of sample weights:
> Intuitively, if all weights are integers, using them in an estimator or a scorer is like duplicating each data point as many times as the weight value.
* It might not always be possible to produce a workable solution for a single-class problem using a binary classifier like in logistic regression here.

title: confusion_matrix crashes when sample_weight is an empty array
body:
### Describe the bug

When calling confusion_matrix with non-empty y_true and y_pred but an empty
sample_weight array, the function crashes during internal processing.

This appears to be caused by inconsistent handling of empty sample_weight
compared to all-zero sample_weight, which currently raises a ValueError.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

y_true = [0, 1]
y_pred = [0, 1]

confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=[])


### Expected Results

Either
A clear ValueError indicating invalid sample_weight, OR
A documented and consistent behavior matching all-zero sample_weight.

In any case, the function should not crash internally.


### Actual Results

The function crashes with an internal error related to array length mismatch
during confusion matrix construction.

Thank you for reporting this issue, @Nitin-Prata, and for your interest in improving scikit-learn.

The [documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix.html) specifies that `sample_weight` must be array-like with shape `(n_samples,)` or `None`. An empty list does not satisfy this requirement when `y_true` and `y_pred` are non-empty.

With that said, I'm closing this issue as "not planned."

title: r2_score() no longer supports `pyarrow.ChunkedArray` inputs
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In `scikit-learn` 1.8.0,`r2_score()` and other metric functions supported `pyarrow.ChunkedArray` input.

With the latest nightlies, they raise a hard-to-understand error from inside `narwhals`.

I suspect this was broken by #31127. Reporting because this showed up in `lightgbm`'s tests using the latest `scikit-learn` nightlies (https://github.com/lightgbm-org/LightGBM/issues/7269).

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Using Python 3.14 just as an example, I don't have any reason to suspect this is sensitive to Python version.

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  -it python:3.14 \
  bash

pip install \
  --prefer-binary \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.anaconda.org/scientific-python-nightly-wheels/simple \
  'cffi>=2.0.0' \

comments.body:
sklearn 1.9+ uses [narwhals](https://narwhals-dev.github.io/) internally: its`check_consistent_length` calls `nw.from_native(x)` without`allow_series=True`, which raises `TypeError` for `pa.ChunkedArray`. 

`pa.ChunkedArray` has no `.shape`, falls through to the narwhals branch, and `nw.from_native(pa_chunked_array)` raises TypeError because narwhals requires `series_only=True` when calling `from_native` on a Series-type. The sklearn PR #31127 introduced the `is_into_dataframe() or is_into_series()` check.

## MCV code for reproduction

Works for `pl.Series` does not work for `pa.ChunkedArray`

```python  
# pip install narwhals pyarrow polars scikit-learn==1.9.dev0 --extra-index-url https://pypi.anaconda.org/scientific-python-nightly-wheels/simple
import narwhals as nw
import pyarrow as pa
import polars as pl

arr = pa.chunked_array([[0, 1, 2, 1, 0]])
series = pl.Series([0, 1, 2, 1, 0])

# 1. narwhals correctly identifies pa.ChunkedArray as a series type
print(nw.dependencies.is_into_series(arr))     # True
print(nw.dependencies.is_into_series(series))  # True

# 2. pl.Series has .shape so sklearn's _num_samples short-circuits BEFORE narwhals
print(hasattr(series, "shape"))  # True  → returns shape[0] immediately, never calls nw.from_native
print(hasattr(arr, "shape"))     # False → falls through to nw.from_native

# 3. pa.ChunkedArray hits nw.from_native — which requires allow_series=True
try:
    nw.from_native(arr)           # raises TypeError
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"from_native no flags: {e}")

nw.from_native(arr, series_only=True)   # works fine
nw.from_native(arr, allow_series=True)  # also works

# 4. Reproduce the sklearn _num_samples failure directly
from sklearn.utils.validation import _num_samples
try:
    _num_samples(arr)    # TypeError — hits buggy narwhals branch
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"_num_samples(pa.ChunkedArray): {e}")

print(_num_samples(series))  # 5 — pl.Series short-circuits before narwhals
```

The bug in sklearn PR #31127 is line 381: `nw.from_native(x)` should be `nw.from_native(x, allow_series=True)`.

---

My primary concern is that sklearn doesn't really support `pa.ChunkedArray / pa.Array` for `y` and most usages always end up using `np.asarray` instead. PyArrow arrays as `y` have never been a declared sklearn input type in their tests either. So, I'm not sure if this is the approach the developers would like to take.

title: RFC Remove possibly unused extra_requires i.e. `pip install scikit-learn[your_thing_goes_here]`
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

This was moved from the setuptools days to pyproject.toml, I don't think anyone is using it but I could be wrong of course.

### What `extra_requires` are useful for

**As a user** you can do for example `pip install scikit-learn[examples]` to be able to run the examples.

**As a developer**, in principle you could do `pip install -e .[tests]` to install everything including test dependencies but I don't think anyone is using it. It is definitely not mentioned in the doc, and I would rather remove all the extra_requires unless someone has a strong use case for it.

### Why they can be removed

They are likely not used by anyone.

Here is a [regex search across GitHub](https://github.com/search?q=%2Fscikit-learn%5C%5B%5Ba-z%5D%2B%5C%5D%2F&type=code) that only shows some matches like `pip install scikit-learn[alldeps]` which is exactly the same as `pip install scikit-learn` (maybe it was different at some time in old history).

The list of existing extra_requires are `build`, `install`, `benchmark`, `docs`, `examples`, `tests`, `maintenance`.

Here is the code showing what each `extra_requires` contains:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4c710ce893600ee655b5b10afd53d9c16da82c33/pyproject.toml#L46-L98

Some are completely broken, e.g. `pip install -e .[build]` as mentioned by @cakedev0 in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34533#issuecomment-5031993769

### What would need to be done

- remove the extra_requires from pyproject.toml
- There are probably some tests somewhere that check min dependencies consistency and that could be removed.
- Also the tags in `sklearn/_min_dependencies.py` (`build`, `maintenance`, etc ...) could maybe be removed? This needs double-checking.

Ping @thomasjpfan in case you have some opinion on this off the top of your head!

###
author: lesteve

comments.body:
Yes, lets remove them from extras. These days we have [dependency groups](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-groups/), which are better for listing out dev dependencies:

```bash
uv pip install --group docs
```

body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm Daniel and I use Scikit-learn both in private projects and at work. I work as a Data Scientist and currently building a personal project.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

So I am working on a data classification project and trying to use one-hot encoding within a pipeline.  I have organised my columns based on the needed impute through SimpleImputer (mean and most frequent). Simple imputer was able to impute where its needed and ignore non-missing columns but One-Hot always encode everything regardless of dtype. And I couldn't avoid that without re-editing my columns even though my groupings work well without repetition. 

### Describe your proposed solution

My proposed solution is to add a `skip` kwarg so the user can select the columns to skip during the process. I believe better solutions could be developed but thats what I am currently thinking.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Could probably use `make_column_selector` but the user still has to manually encode at some point.

### Additional context

_No response_
